MRS. MACINNIS-ANSWER TO QUESTION ON SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT LOAN PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning the manner in which we are being treated in this House by answers to questions with regard to an urgent matter.
Last Friday, in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), I attempted to raise with his parliamentary secretary the serious plight of the cities of Vancouver and Victoria. Before they had submitted their applications under the special development loan fund, the entire sum available to the province of British Columbia had been allocated by the government of British Columbia, despite the fact that some 40 per cent of all those unemployed reside in those two cities. I urged that the minister consider increasing the total amount of the fund for Canada.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, you called me to order, saying that it was your impression that this question had been asked previously. You were quite correct, Mr. Speaker. Several of us had been trying to use this method to impress on the government the urgent need for help for these and other hard-pressed municipalities.
It is quite evident that up to this point the government is washing its hands of this whole matter and giving us the runaround here in the House of Commons.
I am now in receipt of further correspondence from the mayor's office, citing the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) as declaring:
... I would appreciate knowing if you have any difficulty clearing your projects through either the federal government or the provincial co-ordinator.
The mayor also encloses a copy of a letter from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) promising that the Minister of Finance will be in touch "very soon" but declaring that "this is a matter of provincial responsibility".
In view of the way in which Canada's third largest city is being given the brush-off and its representatives are being given the runaround, I feel that this whole matter should be examined by a committee of the House. Accordingly, if you find that I have a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I would be prepared to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch):
That the matter of the administration of the federal-provincial employment loan program be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for immediate study and report.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INTERNATIONAL MONETARY SETTLEMENT AND CONSEQUENCES FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an international monetary settlement was reached on Saturday, and I should like to report on it to the House.
With the permission of the House I will be tabling the communique issued at the end of the meeting of the Group of Ten. The principal features of the agreement may be summarized as follows:
1.	The United States agreed to propose to Congress a devaluation of the dollar in terms of gold from $35 to $38 an ounce. This is an effective change of 8.57 per cent.
2.	For the time being, Canada will maintain a floating exchange rate and will permit fundamental market forces to establish the exchange rate without intervention except as required to maintain orderly conditions.
3.	Other countries in the Group of Ten agreed on new exchange rates for their currencies, and these are being announced by the governments concerned.
4.	Countries other than those in the Group of Ten are reaching decisions with respect to their own exchange rates in consultation with the IMF.
5.	It was agreed that there should be 2-1/4 per cent margins of fluctuations above and below the new fixed exchange rates.
6.	The United States agreed to suppress immediately the 10 per cent import surcharge and the related provisions of the investment tax credit. I am informed that the White House has announced the suppression of the import surcharge with effect from midnight, Sunday, December 19.

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INTERNATIONAL MONETARY SETTLEMENT AND CONSEQUENCES FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

December 20, 1971
International Monetary Settlement

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INTERNATIONAL MONETARY SETTLEMENT AND CONSEQUENCES FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Under the provisions of the Revenue Act of 1971, termination of the proclamation which established the surcharge automatically extends the investment credit to imported capital equipment which is ordered after the date of termination of the surcharge.
7.	The United States administration will be seeking Congressional action on the gold price as soon as the results of the negotiations now under way on short-term trade issues are available for Congressional scrutiny.
8.	Discussions will be undertaken promptly in the IMF on the reform of the international monetary system.
I should like to comment on the significance of this agreement for Canada. On the most general level it restores an orderly exchange situation on the basis of which world trade and financing can proceed with confidence. This will be of benefit to all countries, not least Canada, having in mind the vital importance of international trade to the Canadian economy.
The basis has been laid for the United States to restore its balance of payments to a sound and durable position. A serious obstacle to the expansion of the U.S. economy has been removed. When the United States prospers, Canada prospers also.
The Canadian economy has been advancing at a good pace this year. But the unsettled international situation has given rise to a sense of uncertainty in the business community. This has now been dispelled. We may therefore expect that the Canadian economy will move forward with even greater vigour.
In the field of our international relationships we also have reason to be satisfied. There have been anxieties and doubts about the direction of the United States trade and financial policies and, in particular, about the intention of the United States toward Canada. The agreement reached this weekend should help to remove these tensions. Our other partners in the Group of Ten have demonstrated a full understanding of Canada's position.
I now turn to some more particular questions relating to the consequences for Canada of this agreement.
First, the exchange rate. It will be determined by the fundamental forces in the exchange market. Our interventions will be limited to the maintenance of orderly market conditions. I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that there has been a large turnover in the foreign exchange market today, and the Canadian dollar is trading at precisely what it closed at on Friday last.

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INTERNATIONAL MONETARY SETTLEMENT AND CONSEQUENCES FOR CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FINANCE

speechtext:
I do not expect that the terms of the agreement will have a marked effect on the exchange value of the Canadian dollar. I would stress that the change in the gold price in itself will have no direct effect on the relative value of the American and Canadian dollars.
There are some reasons to expect a stronger growth in our exports. These include the removal of the surcharge and the discriminatory features of the investment tax credit. The appreciation of other currencies will improve our competitive position. But we can also expect a more rapid growth in our imports as a result of the restoration of confidence and a more rapid expansion of Canadian production and investment. The growth of the Canadian
[Mr. Benson.)
economy this year has already been reflected in a more rapid growth of our imports than of our exports and a consequent decline in the trade surplus.
Our policy has been to seek to reduce our imports of capital. I have been asking Canadian borrowers to look to Canadian markets for their needs. I repeat that request today. I continue to believe that it is both practical and appropriate for us to supply more of our financial needs from our own savings.
Second, I would refer to the bilateral discussions of trade questions between Canada and the United States. The monetary agreement demonstrates that these have not been directly related to the United States import surcharge or the realignment of currencies. There are indeed matters of concern to both sides in the trade field. Progress is being made in discussions of these matters, and it is the intention of the government to proceed expeditiously toward a settlement. Canada and the United States are the world's largest trading partners. We hope to get rid of any abrasive elements in our commercial relationships. When the time is ripe, my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), will report to the House on the outcome of these discussions.
Third, the suppression of the United States import surcharge will enable us to wind up the operations of the Employment Support Act.
Mr. Speaker, these negotiations have not been easy. Because of the inherent complexity of the subjects, there have been many meetings-bilateral and multilateral. Officials have met. There have been four meetings of the Group of Ten ministers and governors. I chaired the first two and through the rotation system the last two benefited from the energetic and determined chairmanship of Secretary Connally. Heads of government have met. There is no doubt that the meeting two weeks ago between our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and President Nixon contributed to the satisfactory outcome from the point of view of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON INTERNATIONAL MONETARY SETTLEMENT AND CONSEQUENCES FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) I am pleased and I am sure we are all pleased that a general settlement of the world monetary crisis was achieved at Washington over the weekend. I am also pleased to see that other changes have been made such as the wider spread and more flexibility with regard to the fluctuation of currencies. I am also very pleased to see that the arrangements made did not involve the repegging of the Canadian dollar at a higher level, at this time at least, and, of course, that the United States surtax is going to disappear.
December 20, 1971

There are quite a few questions to be resolved, however. For example, the minister has not made entirely clear how long the Canadian dollar can float under this arrangement. Have we been committed not to intervene under any circumstances with regard to the floating of our dollar? Were any conditions at all attached to the floating of the Canadian dollar or have we acquired some kind of special status in the International Monetary Fund? These are matters on which the minister could perhaps shed some light. I assume the agreement made by this government with the United States a couple of years ago that we would maintain our United States holdings in connection with the exchange fund in non-negotiable securities stands as it was.
We now have a floating dollar, Mr. Speaker, a dollar which floated up from about 92 J cents to 98 j cents at the time President Nixon made his announcement last August with regard to his economic policies. Since mid-August it has floated up about two more cents to about half a cent above par. I would certainly agree with the Minister of Finance that moving up from 92 i cents to something above par is as much as anybody could reasonably expect the Canadian dollar to do. We are all aware, I believe, of the effect that this upward movement has had upon many of our export industries and therefore upon jobs. We must regard increasing the number of jobs in Canada as our No. 1 priority at the present time; certainly we are far from out of the woods in this regard.
One of our concerns, Sir, is whether our dollar will float higher. Will it continue to float upward in relation to the United States dollar? It has done so since August 15, during which time most other world currencies have been moving upward in relation to the United States dollar. Now we are entering a new phase of the upward movement of most currencies. Their value will increase in relation to that of the United States dollar. What assurance is there, therefore, that continued upward floating of the Canadian dollar will not take place, as has been the case since mid-August of this year? The Minister of Finance says that the value of the Canadian dollar ought not to move upward at all in relation to the value of the United States dollar. However, that has been the trend, and the United States Secretary of the Treasury seems to have said precisely the opposite to what the Minister of Finance has said. Others are expressing concern. I am concerned myself. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this time the Minister of Finance is right.

speechtext: It will be the first time.

subtopic: FINANCE

speechtext:
I am certainly pleased, as I say, to see that the Canadian dollar has not been pegged at a higher rate, but I emphasize, of course, that the mere fact our dollar is floating will not provide for us anything like Utopia. There is a very real danger that we will get into the same fix if the dollar floats higher than we would have got into if the dollar had been pegged at a higher rate.
Again, Sir, we do not yet know the price we will have to pay for the arrangement that was worked out over the weekend. Were concessions made with regard to other irritants such as the auto pact? The Minister of Finance has said no. But the more relevant question is, will the
International Monetary Settlement
United States be particularly tough on Canada in these other areas such as the auto pact? The Minister of Finance said that what happened over the weekend shows that many of our fears regarding the United States attitude toward Canada were groundless. With great respect to the minister, I do not think we have yet got the answer to that question. Many of us will be concerned about just how tough the attitude of the United States administration will now be in areas like the auto pact.
We have not returned to the pre-August era. As I said, our dollar has risen in value by about 2 per cent since the middle of August, and there are still pressures around to push it up. The so-called DISC program is still on the books. For all we know, it will soon come into effect. The government is unable to tell us what the effect of that program will be upon Canada and what contingency plans it may announce. The government has no general development strategy. The minister spoke about this settlement increasing the confidence of the business community. If he is so concerned about confidence, he might take a look at some of the domestic policies this government is pursuing-

-which will have a substantial effect in diminishing the desire of people to commit money for investment.
The air of secrecy about these whole discussions is regrettable. I must say that I know more about what has been going on in the Common Market countries than about what has been going on in Canada in relation to these discussions with the United States.
Finally, without taking too much time may I say to the minister that I recognize that this must have been a time of great anxiety and pressure for him. I am pleased that a general settlement has been reached and I am pleased that he reached the objective he sought in connection with these discussions, a floating dollar. I am concerned, however, about what the achievement of this objective will mean for Canada, about what it will mean to the movement of our dollar and about what it will mean for employment in this country. I am concerned about these matters. Certainly we do not yet know what price will be exacted from this country for having been permitted to leave our dollar afloat. I can best describe my state of mind by saying that I am in a state of hopeful scepticism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nothing could demonstrate the failure of the policies of the Canadian government in any attempts it may have made to develop a viable and independent economy in Canada more than one short paragraph in the minister's statement. I quote that paragraph:
The basis has been laid for the United States to restore its balance of payments to a sound and durable position. A serious obstacle to the expansion of the U.S. economy has been removed. When the United States prospers, Canada prospers also.
That is a damning indictment of the policies of the Canadian government as we witnessed them over the past 10 to 15 years.
It is fine for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to come before us today and say that the United States balance of payments and its economy are in a sound and

December 20, 1971
International Monetary Settlement
durable position. What we are interested in is the state of the Canadian economy. What is the situation in Canada?
The minister starts off by saying that "when the United States prospers, Canada prospers also." In the next paragraph he shows the government's compliance with that sort of point of view. He deals with the Canadian economy and, with his usual bravado, he comes forward and says: "We may therefore expect that the Canadian economy will move forward with even greater vigour." If that statement had come from any other minister on the government benches, it would have had some credibility. However, coming from the Minister of Finance, with his record regarding forecasts, this statement is not worth the paper on which it is written.
We also have to ask what deals were made behind the scene, what concessions were made and what understandings have been reached which may not yet be in writing? At one point in his statement the minister reported that progress has been made in trade talks. This can only mean that there have been some concessions. It probably means there was some horse-trading in these trade talks. Whatever concessions and adjustments have been made are of critical importance to many thousands of Canadians with regard to their everyday livelihood.
There is no doubt that to some extent the immediate impact of the announcements made today and in the last couple of days will be to relieve some stress and anxieties with regard to the economic situation, but for the long run we have no answers. I say quite frankly that none of us expects to have all of the answers now. None of us expected all of these problems to be solved by this time. But we do need to have a better idea of in what direction government policy is moving and in what direction Canada is moving.
What is the government doing to develop long-run trade policies? The minister states there are reasons to expect a stronger growth in our exports. We would like to know what exports. Is this going to be a case of continued growth in exports of our natural resources, our primary resources? The latest trade figures which have been released, for the month of November, indicate that this is the case. We are exporting more and more of our raw materials. This is becoming a greater proportion of our trade.
We also take note of the fact that talks are being held with the United States. Of critical importance to Canada, of course, is the question of our relationship with that country. This is one of the questions with which we must grapple in dealing with our long-run trade policy. Up to the present time the government has followed a policy of commiting Canada to dependency on the United States greater than many of us would like to see.
The minister reports progress in dealing with certain irritants. We would like to know which ones-the auto pact, defence sharing or some of the other irritants which have been referred to from time to time during the discussions? What options is the government exploring with respect to the future direction and thrust of trade policy? Will the government continue on the simplistic course of simply looking for global tariff reductions, desirable as these might be? Are we to strengthen our relationships

with some of the trading groups? Just where is Canada going in its trade policy? None of us can find out at the present time.
I note that the minister also commented on our international investment position. He says in his statement: "I have been asking Canadian borrowers to look to Canadian markets for their needs; I repeat that request today." The point I must make is that this is a step to curtail the wrong aspect of the flow of capital into Canada. What the minister is attempting to do is to restrict the inflow of borrowed capital into Canada rather than equity capital. I think all of us recognize that there are occasions on which some flow of capital into Canada is required. But the point must be made that to the extent that we must rely on imports of capital, that capital should be in the form of borrowed capital rather than equity capital. It is obvious that the minister is moving in the wrong direction.
The minister has told us that the surcharge has been removed, as well as the discriminatory features of the investment tax credit. We must also ask the question: What about the DISC legislation, what about the legislation concerning domestic international sales corporations? Where are we moving in this regard? Are there to be any changes in United States policy in this area?
I note the minister's comments to the effect that Canada will continue to operate a floating exchange rate. We certainly approve this decision, as we have for some time. But we are also concerned about what commitments might have been made in this respect. What concessions were made in this regard? I note one item which appeared in the Globe and Mail this morning-

by the Minister of Finance, I think there is a long dark winter ahead for many thousands of Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I perused the statement of the Minister of Finance only a few minutes before the House met, when I received the English text together with a memorandum explaining why we did not get the French text. I therefore accept the minister's apologies and I am sure he did his very best.
The minister's statement is brief, and so will mine be. It shows that with some goodwill it is possible to alter the monetary system, once it has been decided to do so. We have once more the proof that it is men who control money. This is a statement to be remembered, and which the people will be able to understand.
The devaluation of the American dollar and the reevaluation of the currencies of other countries, while allowing the Canadian dollar to continue to float, show clearly that changes are necessary in the financial field in order to prevent economic disasters. The time has come for action; I hope that it is not too late and that it is still possible to repair the damage.
I am happy to learn that the American surtax will surely disappear. We will then be able to see whether this policy is liable to improve the Canadian economy so that the whole country may benefit.
However, I deplore the fact that our economy should to such an extent depend on that of the United States. I suggest that we should never let up in our efforts to establish our economy on a more solid basis, so that it be less dependent on the American economy and more on the potential of the domestic market.
We could-and such is the wish that I express for the New Year-make another reform which, further to providing Canadians with a higher minimum income, would boost their purchasing power so as to enable them to buy a greater part of Canadian production. We would thus ensure a better distribution of goods and a greater degree of independence in relation to export markets.
And were that wish to materialize, I would be able to say at the end of 1972 that it was the best year for the Canadian government and for Canadian consumers.

subtopic: SURVEY OF RADIOACTIVITY IN COLOUR TV SETS
speechtext:
1. In 1969, the Department of National Health and Welfare conducted a survey of about 500 privately-owned colour TV sets to determine the extent of X-ray emission.
2.	Approximately $6,000.
3.	The results of the survey were published in a scientific report available from the Department. Summary findings were disseminated to the media through news releases.
4.	About 11 per cent of the colour TV sets tested were found to emit radiation somewhat above the recommended level. In view of this, the Department, through the media, recommended to the public TV habits that would avoid any possible harm.
5.	It was determined that the excess radiation levels were largely caused by deficiencies in certain components. Subsequently, these were greatly improved by the Industry. Regulations governing design, construction and performance to ensure safety have been developed by the Department and are expected to be in force soon under the Radiation Emitting Devices Act.

speechtext:

Is it the intention of the government to redesign and rearrange the Green Gables Golf Course in the Prince Edward Island National Park and, if so, has any survey been carried out among persons who regularly golf on this course or among local residents as to the desirability of the proposed change and with what result?

Hon. ]ean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development): 1. The National and Historic Parks Branch is presently engaged in a number of planning studies of Prince Edward Island National Park, particularly in the Cavendish area. Some of the alternative planning proposals being considered do involve modifications to the Green Gables Golf Course. 2. In anticipation of this need the National and Historic Parks Branch is engaged in acquiring additional land which would facilitate any modifications to the golf course should they prove necessary.
3.	Since planning studies are only in the initial stages and several alternatives are involved it is not possible at this time to make any estimation of cost related to possible golf course modifications.

Mr. Speaker, I do not have a lengthy comment to make on the bill at the present time. It contains three amendments of substance to the Excise Tax Act. There are also amendments to the Old Age Security Act and to the Excise Tax Act in order to provide that the 3 percentage point of sales tax now imposed as an Old Age Security tax will, in future, be imposed under the Excise Tax Act. The amendments planned to the Excise Tax Act provide, first, that machinery and apparatus sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers for purposes of reducing pollution are made exempt from sales tax; second, margarine and similar spreads are made exempt from sales tax and, thirdly, the special excise tax of 15 per cent on radios, television sets and electron tubes, is repealed. The amendment to the Old Age Security Act will repeal the 3 per cent Old Age Security tax on sales imposed under that act. However, these 3 percentage points of tax will in future be imposed under the Excise Tax Act and this change will not result in any change in the total rate of sales tax.

speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think we shall have a slow and desultory discussion on this particular bill. These items were introduced so long ago that I think most members of the House have forgotten that these measures actually exist. They have now come back to be considered at, shall we say, the fifty ninth minute before midnight.
The amendment is designed, first of all, to remove the excise tax on margarine. I remember thinking at the time of the budget that perhaps a freer use of margarine might make the contents of the budget and subsequent bills slide down, so to speak, a lot more easily. In any event, there will not be much saving. It is a question of whether or not savings that might have been effected by the manufacturers and retailers have been passed on to the consumer. Whether or not that saving has been passed on is a good question. We do not know whether the price of margarine reflects the exact change that was introduced in the budget. I have not canvassed the market to see whether the price of margarine is lower than it would have been if this particular provision had not been included in the budget. I thought the tax on margarine was an unsound tax and I am glad to see that it has gone. I thought it was an anachronism to have such a tax on a generally accepted foodstuff. It was imposed in the past in order to protect the dairy industry. I recall many years ago reading of the initial results of the bill that was brought in to this House from the other place and sponsored, I believe, by Senator Isnor. That bill legalized the sale of margarine in this country.
The one item I wish to talk about is the elimination of the excise tax on those items that are enumerated under paragraph 5 of the Ways and Means motion or section 4 of the bill. I believe the minister has given me a proper private explanation. The existing bill has come about as a result of the proclamation of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1971. The ways and means motion was based on the law as it then existed. This House passed the ways and means resolution on the law as it then existed, but sometime around July 15 the Revised Statutes of Canada 1971 were proclaimed. This effected a consolidation of what had heretofore been paragraph 5 of Section 1. It is now paragraph 4 of Section 1.
I think the point of order I raised has now had sufficient explanation. The question is, did the removal of the excise tax on these particular items, phonographs, record playing devices, radio-broadcasting receiving sets and combinations of these, television receiving sets, electronic tubes and other related items, have the effect which the minister hoped? I would like to have some information on this from the parliamentary secretary. Perhaps when we are discussing this in detail he will be able to tell us what expansion there has been of the market for the sale of these particular electronic devices. Have television sets sold in greater numbers? Has the price come down to reflect the removal of the sales tax, not 15 per cent of the retail price but 15 per cent of the manufacturer's price? If there has been a reduction in price, has there been a stimulation of sales? If there has been a stimulation of sales, has this been reflected in an increase in domestic production as hoped for by the minister? It will be the

height of folly if, by the removal of this tax, all we do is stimulate the Japanese television industry. This could really be the result.
As we know, there are any number of television sets sold in this country under perfectly good Canadian names? The people believe they are made in Canada. However, they are actually made in Japan. If there has been an increase in sales as a result of the removal of the 15 per cent sales tax at the manufacturer's level, and we have seen no increase in production by Canadian manufacturers, what is the purpose of the exercise? All we have done has been to offer to the Japanese electronics industry a potentially lower market price to further penetrate the Canadian market. We need a full explanation of this.
We like to see tax reductions. True enough, people with lower incomes may benefit to the extent that small radio sets will have the 15 per cent sales tax removed from them. They benefit to that extent. I suppose many of them buy television sets, perhaps not the more expensive makes, but are they Canadian made? It was claimed that this was to be a stimulus to make Canadian industry more competitive. If the sales tax is not payable on an imported set, the actual saving on the retail price of an imported set will actually be more than the tax on the manufacturer's cost because the sales tax is on the duty paid value. There is no mention about reducing customs duty on these particular imported sets. The sales tax is actually effected at a higher level on an imported set than on a domestic set. I repeat, I would like this information from the parliamentary secretary.
There is some shifting around. Instead of the 3 per cent sales tax imposed by the Old Age Security Act and earmarked for the old age security fund, we are now getting a flat 12 per cent sales tax. The minister or the parliamentary secretary should give the House a full explanation as to how the old age security fund is to be funded from the 12 per cent put into the consolidated revenue fund or whatever it may be. After all, the old age security fund was supposed to have been contributed to by all persons. It was deemed to be a pension based on a fund that was to be contributed to by all segments of the population.
If there is a 3 per cent sales tax specifically earmarked for the old age security fund, every person who buys commodities in the Canadian market, except for most food items and until June 18, margarine, will contribute to that fund. However, unless it is specifically earmarked for the old age security fund, then individuals will feel that as far as they are concerned, it is no longer contributory. The taxpayer had certain rights at one time, but no longer. Under Bill C-259, we have a completely all encompassing provision. The funding of the old security fund will be strictly from the consolidated revenue fund. Presumably, it will be on an as needed basis.
There has been a removal or an expansion of the removal of sales tax on anti-pollution equipment. To that extent I say congratulations to the government. We can easily encourage much more anti-pollution effort by the way of incentives such as the removal of tax on certain equipment that will be used to control pollution, particularly in water and in the air. I suppose one could say that the proposals of this bill are counterproductive. They remove the sales tax on certain radios and other electronic equipment which, frankly, are among the greatest noise pollu-
December 20, 1971

tants in this modern day. As a result, we are now asked to remove sales tax from equipment which will be used to control or eliminate pollution. Noise pollution is not mentioned in this particular section, otherwise they might double the tax on certain types of transistor radios and a few other loudspeaker items, particularly on those loudspeakers which amplify so-called musical sounds and which will crack glass and split plaster.
I feel there is a great deal to be gained by extensive discussion on second reading. I have drawn attention to the areas with which I should like the parliamentary secretary to deal. Then we shall proceed, in due course, to committee of the whole.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the parliamentary secretary has pointed out, the substantial part of this bill is to be found in those clauses which remove the excise tax from certain indicated commodities. For the most part, we welcome these changes. But in any case the discussion of the changes with respect to the excise tax on commodities will be entered into by two or three of my colleagues. I propose to spend my time on the second reading of this bill on the part of the measure which the parliamentary secretary said involved no real change, namely, that part dealing with the amendments to the Old Age Security Act.
I think it is necessary to relate the provisions in this bill, Bill C-260, in this regard, to the provisions of Bill C-259 which also have the effect of amending the Old Age Security Act. If we put these two together, clause 3 of C-259 and clause 5 of C-260, as well as some of the other clauses in this bill, we find that a substantial change is being made with regard to the manner in which taxes are collected for old age security. Although I accept the word of the parliamentary secretary to the effect that substantial tax changes are in the other parts of this bill, I think something substantial is being done with regard to the method of financing old age security.
Whenever taxes are eliminated or reduced one is usually expected to applaud. I might go further and say that when a change is made from a regressive to a progressive form of taxation one is expected to applaud. If I thought this was all that was happening in this case I would make my applause very evident, and sit down. But I confess I am consumed with a deep suspicion as to what is happening in connection with this matter. My suspicion is heightened by the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in his budget speech of June 18, did not make a single reference to this matter. He did not even say a change was being made. Only the tabling of the ways and means motion drew it to our attention. I thought the hon. gentleman presenting this bill on behalf of the government might have explained why this change in the method of taxation relating to old age security was being put into effect. But not a word was said. I did not even find anything about it in the red book containing a summary of the changes made in our tax legislation-if the hon. gentleman can tell me I have missed it, I shall be pleased to accept that advice.
Up till now, money has been obtained from the old age security fund-from which payments of old age security
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
benefits are made-from three sources of taxation. There has been a 4 per cent tax on personal income with a ceiling of $240 a year as the most which can be paid. Second, there has been a 3 per cent tax on corporation income, and, third, there has been a sales tax of 3 per cent for old age security purposes. That 3 per cent has been part of the total sales tax, whether it is 11 per cent or 12 per cent, depending on what commodities are in question. In any event, the revenue from these three percentage points of sales tax has gone into the old age security fund. The Old Age Security Act has provided that in the event of there being a deficit in the old age security fund the Minister of Finance can make certain loans to the fund, and so on, but this has not happened for a long time. As a matter of fact, the fund was running with a credit balance of $687 million as of October, 1971, the last figure available to me.
I should like to make it clear that we opposed from the start the regressive nature of much of this old age security taxation. We felt it was regressive to impose a flat tax of 4 per cent-first it was 2 per cent, then it was 3 per cent, and latterly it was 4 per cent-on all income rather than impose a graduated tax. We pointed out that this had the effect of placing a disproportionate burden on those in the lower income brackets. We had no quarrel with placing a 3 per cent tax on corporations, but we did object to the sales tax being used, because, again, we felt this was taxing those in the lower income brackets to a disproportionate extent. This having been our position and since it has also been a fact of history that we have repeatedly tried to get the ceiling raised, I can understand that hon. members opposite will say: why are you now complaining when the 4 per cent tax on personal income has been removed, when the tax on corporations has been removed and when the three percentage points which were collected for old age security will no longer be collected for that purpose? The reason I am questioning all this is that I have been around here for a while and have learned to be suspicious of things that Liberals do, at least when they are in power. I find myself applauding the Liberals very strongly if they are on the opposition side of the House, but when they get over on the government side they do some strange things.
I think it is necessary that I point out that when the present Old Age Security Act was passed in 1951, and became law in 1952, it was passed on the basis of a report made by a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons, a report on old age security tabled on June 28, 1950. I well remember the work we did in this committee. Some very distinguished people were members and I think the committee did an excellent job. It was this committee that recommended the removal of the means test from the old age pension, which was to be paid to everyone at age 70, which was the figure then, and amounted to $40 a month, as well as providing old age assistance for those between 65 and 69. I am happy to say that we have done a good deal since then in terms of improvement, such as getting the amount up and the age limit down. But the heart of our report of 1950 was its recommendation of universality.

December 20, 1971
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
In the course of our recommendations we dealt with the question of how the new universal pension was to be financed. At page 110 of the report, paragraph 64 reads as follows:
The Committee is in favour of the contributory principle, not only because of the importance of this in raising total moneys required, but also because of the importance of establishing a close association in the mind of the individual between his contribution to the cost and the ultimate benefit he is to receive.
Although the members of the committee differed as to the rates of tax that should be imposed and that sort of thing, we were unanimous that there should be a contributory element in paying for old age security so that the Canadian people would know that they had contributed toward their pension and would be able to say the pension was theirs as a matter of right. Just interrupting my train of thought for a moment, since I am looking at this report perhaps I might also say that the committee in 1950 realized that in order to put in this kind of scheme a contributory arrangement it could well be necessary to amend the British North America Act. This was dealt with in paragraphs 71 and 72 of the report, and as a result of this recommendation an amendment to the British North America Act was passed. We now have section 94, which makes it possible for the federal Parliament, as well as the provincial legislatures, to legislate in the field of old age pensions.
The reason we made this recommendation, and that Parliament accepted it in 1951, was that we were making this change. Previous to that time old age pensions under the previous Old Age Pensions Act were simply paid out of the general revenue; there was no contributory element at all, and therefore no special authority was required. However, it was fully accepted that if we were going to establish a contributory relationship there would have to be authority for it in the British North America Act. This recommendation was made in 1950, and as I say it was accepted by Parliament in 1951.
So that from that time until the present the principle, the philosophy, the rationale, has been clear: the Canadian people make payments that are earmarked for old age security, and those payments go into the old age security fund. It is true that accounts for each individual are not kept separately, as is the case with the Canada Pension Plan, but the contributory relationship is there since all our people have made payments. Therefore, when the time comes to draw his pension each Canadian can say that this pension is his as of right, that he has paid for it not only by his contribution to the economy of the country as a whole but by the specific taxes he has paid.
I may say that this is further confirmed by a few of the statements made in the white paper entitled "Income Security for Canadians" which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) tabled in the House toward the end of 1970. At page 24 of the white paper the following statement appears:
Yet it would not be easy simply to scrap these programs.
One of the programs referred to there is old age security.
Many people have tailored their retirement incomes and made their retirement plans in the expectation that the Old Age Security pension would be paid them from age 65 on. This program has almost the nature of a separate social contract between the state

and its citizens. It has been financed in part since 1952 by a highly visible earmarked personal income tax. It provides the basis for the retirement plans of almost all Canadians regardless of income levels. Private pension arrangements, and the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans, have built benefit structures on the assumption that this payment will be made.
I realize that in that paragraph the minister was dealing with certain other arguments, but he confirmed the philosophy, the rationale, that is behind old age security, namely that there are earmarked payments going into the old age security fund, and that all our people have the benefit of a social contract. People can say, when it is time for them to go on old age pension, that the pension is theirs as a matter of right.
At page 42 of this same white paper, referring to suggestions that some people were making that the Old Age Security Act might be wiped out and replaced by something else, the white paper has this to say:
To withdraw it now would force a reconsideration of retirement benefit levels under those Plans.
The reference there is to the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. I continue:
Many people have planned their retirement on the expectation that they will get Old Age Security at age 65, and to deny them this benefit would be extremely unfair and a breach of faith. Personal income taxes as well as other earmarked taxes have been collected from people since 1952 to finance this program, establishing an expectation and a right to the pension. Under these circumstances, action to restrict the program's universality would be difficult to justify.
In that statement the Minister of National Health and Welfare fends off any suggestion to do away with old age security for, among other reasons, the important one that it is a social contract, that there is an element of faith, that people are making earmarked payments and therefore have a complete moral right to draw their pensions, and to enjoy them, as I say, not as a form of charity but as a matter of right.
If we were dealing with the question of rates, it is quite true that I would still have something critical to say about the ungraduated nature of the tax, the regressive nature of the sales tax, and so on. However, I am dealing with the basic principle whether or not there should be a contributory relationship between the taxes people pay and the old age pension that they draw. When all the changes are made that are now in contemplation, those that are in Bill C-259 which has gone over to the other place and those in this bill now before us, there will not be any more earmarked taxes going into the old age security fund.
My friend, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) expressed the hope that someone speaking for the government would tell us what is going to happen. I had hoped that explanation would be given before we became involved in this debate. This is part of what bothers me, the silence on this issue. No one has attempted to explain it. With all respect to my good friend the parliamentary secretary who did a good job in defending the government's position on Bill C-259, this should have been a ministerial statement. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) should be here, too, because what will happen is that the entire section 24 of the Old Age Security Act will be wiped out. That is the section
December 20, 1971

which provides for the collection of the three taxes, the personal tax, the corporation tax and the sales tax.
The section that provides for an old age security fund still exists. It is there. There is still to be a fund into which certain money will go and out of which pensions will be paid. What money is to go into that fund? So far as I can ascertain, the only money to go into that fund is that which is referred to in clause 3 of Bill C-259 which says that once a year the Minister of National Revenue shall make an estimate concerning how much would have been collected in personal and corporation income taxes if the old earmarked law had been in effect. That estimate having been made, that amount of money is to be turned over by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to the old age security fund. There is one sense in which I like that and I believe I said so in respect of Bill C-259. This means that the money put into the old age security fund will be collected out of general revenue coming more along the line of ability to pay than in the other way. What bothers me, however, is that there is no money going into the old age security fund which individuals can say is money they put there. There is no earmarked contribution whatsoever.
As I say, according to clause 3 of Bill C-259 the Minister of National Revenue is required to make an estimate of how much would have been collected had the old law been in effect. But the old law in that respect is confined to the personal and corporation income tax. There is nothing anywhere which says that anything which would have been collected under the sales tax is to go into the old age security fund. So, from here on the only money going into the old age security fund will be the estimate of what would have been collected from the personal and corporation income taxes. To me there are two or three dangers about that. In the first place, there will be less money. After all, the take from only two taxes will be less than that from three taxes. Second, the earmarked situation, the clarity of relationship, will be gone. Third-and this is what I am afraid of and this is why I am suspicious-it would seem to me the government could well be laying the foundation for being able to say a few years from now, "Oh, well, old age security is just paid out of general revenue and this notion you used to have that you were entitled to it because of contributory payments is gone."
This will put the government in the position of being able to play fast and loose with the whole question of old age security and even abolish its universality. I hope I am wrong in this suspicion, but if there is good reason for all of this, if there is a philosophy behind it which can be exposed, why did the minister not say so on June 18 or when we were debating Bill C-259, because part of this is in clause 3 of that bill, or why did he not say so today and why is not the Minister of National Health and Welfare here to tell us what he thinks about this. It is only a year ago that the Minister of National Health and Welfare tabled his white paper on income security for Canadians. He accepted the fact, and in fact asserted, that one of the cardinal principles of old age security is that it is a social contract, that there is an element of faith between the people and the state and that because of that social contract and because payments are made by individuals on
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
an earmarked basis, they have the right to count on old age security always being there.
Entirely apart from arguments I might make about the desirability of increasing the basic amount of the old age security, which is presently $80,-and everybody knows where I stand on that-I think there is particular merit in the point made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his white paper to the effect that the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan are based on old age security as a first deck. In fact, this was said at page 42 of the white paper:
It is proposed that the old age security pension continue to be payable to people who meet the residence requirements when they reach age 65.
For both the social insurance system and the guaranteed income system, the flat-rate old age security pension will continue to provide the base on which the second deck is built. In the former case the second deck is the earnings-related pension, in the latter it is the income-tested pension. But both are predicated on the continuing existence of the basic old age security payment for all who meet the residence requirements.
That is crucial and fundamental. Whatever changes we may make, whatever progress we may achieve in the field of old age security, we at least now have this basic first deck of $80 a month. Then we have the second deck, the Canada Pension Plan, and all the private pension plans and the other arrangements that people make. The Minister of National Health and Welfare was perfectly right in his white paper when he said that the people of Canada have a right to expect that first deck to remain. What was one of the main reasons he gave that we have the right to expect that first deck to remain? Because it was in the nature of a social contract and because the people are making earmarked contributory payments. To do anything to disturb that would be a breach of faith. Can you not see, Sir, that if all these earmarked taxes are removed, this philosophy begins to fade and a few years from now some government which wants to cut down on old age security, or put it on an income test, could say, "Well, it is just a payment made out of the general revenue". They would say there are no more earmarked taxes for it and so they are cutting it down. I think that before this debate is over we should have a statement on this. I would be quite happy to see my suspicions completely shot down, but they will not be shot down by silence on the government side but only by someone like the Minister of National Health and Welfare coming in and making clear that so far as he is concerned this change in the taxation basis for old age security does not have that kind of serious defect.
Back a few years, and in fact over a number of years, some of us argued that there was sufficient money in the old age security fund to pay much higher pensions under the Old Age Security Act. When we used to do that we were met with various answers. One was that the new programs that were being brought in, such as the guaranteed income supplement and so on, would soon eat up any surplus. But the figures I have on what is happening to the old age security fund show that over the past couple of years the balance at credit in that fund has not changed very much. It has gone in the last couple of years from a low of about $686 million to a high of about $730 million. But in round figures that is not much of a change, and if one looks at what happens each month, some months there is a surplus of collections over the amount paid out,

December 20, 1971
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
and some months the amount paid out is in excess of the amount brought in.
In other words, I think it is correct to say that at present the taxes coming in from the three sources just about equal what is required to pay, on a month to month basis, the old age security payments and the guaranteed income supplement payments that are also paid out of that fund. We have said in the past that with the extra $687 million that was there at the last report this could be used to increase the payments. The argument that it would be eaten up by the guaranteed income supplement has not worked out, so I suppose now the government feels it is better to cut this fund down so that we will not be able to continue that argument. If you take away these three percentage points of the sales tax, it will not be long before this fund starts to go down. Then we will get some minister of finance or some minister of national health and welfare coming before us and saying that the fund is dropping, that it is just a welfare measure anyway, and we can lose what is a very important social gain, namely old age pensions on a universal basis.
As I have said, if the government can come in with a ringing speech by the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) who is the one who can ring the changes and bring down the rafters, and prove to me that my suspicions are completely groundless, I would be very happy. But it will take that to do it. Silence will not convince me; in fact, it is the silence that has disturbed me. Not a word has been said about this. The parliamentary secretary rose today with a statement which I suppose was prepared for him as a departmental explanation of what this is all about. It just says that some changes are being made in the three percentage points that had been collected under the Old Age Security Act which will now be collected under the Excise Tax Act. There was no explanation or defence of it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said nothing about it on June 18 or when he introduced Bill C-259, and we have heard nothing about it today on Bill C-260. The whole question of the future of old age security is wrapped up in this. I imagine some members are wondering how a bill having to do with the Excise Tax Act produces all this discussion on old age security, but, as Your Honour has recognized, it is in the bill and it is a very substantial change which alters the whole base.
I remind you again, Sir, of the references which I have drawn to your attention. The basic philosophy was set out in the report of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Old Age Security in 1950.1 remind you of the philosophy that was set out in the white paper tabled by the Minister of National Health and Welfare late in 1970 from which it was very clear that the reason people have the right to expect old age security to continue and the right to take these payments with a feeling of pride and honour is that, in addition to any contribution they have made to the economy as a whole, they have contributed earmarked taxes to a special fund.
I want to see some great improvements in the whole matter of old age security. I want to see the guaranteed annual income at a much higher level. I want to see it extended to certain groups, perhaps to housewives, to

veterans, and to others whom I could name. But in the meantime let us not nibble away at what we have. I am afraid that the changes involved in Bill C-259 and Bill C-260 with respect to the financing of old age security have the effect of changing it from a contributory plan which gives all the rights there are to the people to a welfare plan because it will be paid out of revenues collected in a general way rather than revenues collected on an earmarked basis.
I know I am repeating myself but I feel very strongly about this. Everybody knows now how we pay old age security, out of the 4 per cent tax on personal income with a ceiling of $240 a year, plus a 3 per cent corporation income, plus the three percentage points that are built into the sales tax. The effect of these two bills will be to do away with the 4 per cent tax. There will be no more corporation tax, no more of any part of the sales tax going into the old age security fund, and therefore the whole position of people being able to say they are contributing to this pension which is theirs as a matter of right will be vitiated.
If the removal of the three percentage points from the Excise Tax Act so far as the old age security is concerned meant a reduction of the sales tax from 12 per cent and 11 per cent down to 9 per cent and 8 per cent, perhaps there would be something to crow about on the government side, but the sales tax rates are not being changed; the 12 per cent and 11 per cent continue. It does mean that the entire take from the sales tax will now go into the general revenue and none of it will go into the old age security fund. As I said a while ago, the removal of the personal and corporation taxes is at least matched by the requirement that the Minister of National Revenue once a year estimate what the take would have been. That much money must be paid into the old age security fund. But in the case of the sales tax there is no such provision. In other words, the government will have to put all the sales tax receipts into the general fund.
In so far as there is a shift from a regressive to a progressive way of taxation, of course I welcome it, and in so far as the personal income taxes that are used for this are those out of the general structure so that those in the upper brackets pay more than those in the lower, again I welcome that. But in so far as the contributing relationship is being completely wiped out, in so far as the philosophy of 1950 right down to 1970 is being denied by this legislation, I do not like it.
In due course we shall have the committee of the whole stage when we can consider the clauses, when the government can bring its people in here to answer questions, if it will and then third reading. I will be a very happy member if I can be shown that I am wrong, that I have nothing to be afraid of, but it looks to me as though the ground is being prepared for changes in the old age security so that it can no longer be said that individual Canadians have, among other reasons, the right to their old age pensions because they have contributed to these special funds.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) says that this will just become a transfer of payments. As I said earlier, some of my colleagues will deal with the other phases of this bill. Some of them may deal with this phase as well, and I hope they will, but they will be
December 20, 1971

dealing with the changes of tax on spreads, on radios and televisions, on anti-pollution equipment, and so on. I want to say to the parliamentary secretary and to the government that I regard these changes being made in the methods of financing old age security as very important. I am disturbed most of all by the fact that, up to the present time, not one word has been said from the government side about these changes. We have a right to know what these changes really mean.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take advantage of this debate to make a suggestion to the government about Bill C-260.
I should like to bring up, in particular, two points concerning clause 4 on page 2 which deals with apparatus used in the fight against air and water pollution. I feel that the government could have, at the outset, gone a bit further in that field.
I have here a news release from the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities at the time when Mayor Marcel D'Amour was president, in which it was pointed out that the municipalities too have duties with regard to the fight against pollution of all kinds, but that up to now the federal government has failed to encourage municipalities willing to fight it.
I would add that the minister said in the House on June 18 that in order to favour the purchase of equipment used against pollution, he was going to remove immediately the sales tax on it. Such new exemption would apply, according to him, to all kinds of machines which manufacturers or producers buy for use in the detection, prevention, removal or reduction of pollution, but it would reduce revenues by about $8 million a year.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has a part to play in that fight and that the government should have extended the tax exemption to the equipment which municipalities must use for that purpose.
I should also like to call the attention of the minister or of his parliamentary secretary to this point. They will have to read Hansard because I notice they are both absent from the House at this time. As reported in the press, they are fighting air pollution.
We all know that in the construction area, more and more people are using electricity for home heating. In the province of Quebec, Hydro-Quebec, which supplies electricity, is doing a great deal of advertising to push the use of electricity for home heating, since it is a way of fighting air pollution.
I have here an advertisement published in almost every newspaper; it appeared in Montreal-Matin of September 22 1971.1 quote:
Electricity means no combustion, no smoke, no soot no smell,

Hydro-Quebec researchers are continuously improving the methods for producing, transporting and distributing electricity.
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
They are looking for new ways to use it. Everywhere the future is electric. Hydro-Quebec is working for you. Electricity is clean and efficient and it can be used in many ways.
Mr. Speaker, their publicity is trying to encourage people to use electricity to heat their homes, because it does not create pollution.
I know personally several people who reacted to that appeal and who switched to an electrical heating system or who are now installing such a system in new houses.
To my knowledge it costs some $500, $600 or even $700 to set up an electrical heating system in a house. People complain about the high cost of housing and the government, through the Central Mortgate and Housing Corporation, is trying by all possible means to reduce it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) should include in that clause of Bill C-260 a provision to exempt all materials used for electric heating systems in dwellings.
The construction cost of family dwellings could thus be reduced and the new owners would pay less for a house. The monthly payments would be decreased, because for an average 2 or 3 bedroom-house the taxes on building materials would be $75 or $100 lower.
Mr. Speaker, I urge this government to further consider this suggestion and to grant an exemption concerning electrical home heating. This would benefit all homeowners, all Canadian families and, at the same time, it would be an efficient way to fight pollution.
This government, the minister and his officials should, as soon as possible, consider this proposal. I myself have considered moving an amendment to Bill C-260 to that effect. But, after study, any amendment that I might have moved on that subject would have been ruled out of order.
That is why I shall wait for another opportunity to move an amendment or a motion on this subject.
In my view, the government should immediately give consideration to that possibility and, during the study in committee of the whole, we shall see if it is possible to move an amendment with regard to this matter.

subtopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subsubtopic: CONSEQUENTLY NO POLLUTION. ELECTRICITY IN QUEBEC IS CLEAN AND EFFICIENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I must say that I am slightly disappointed that many of the questions raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) have not been answered. Hon. members continue to wonder just what is the intention with respect to the actual application of the clauses in the bill.
Dealing first with clause 1, and the transfer of the 3 per cent from the sales tax to the excise tax, one wonders whether the suspicions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are well founded. I can recall that upon the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan there was much discussion on whether the old age security pension should be dropped since, with payment of the Canada Pension Plan benefits, it possibly could be eliminated. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) made a statement to the effect that today many old people consider that they have a contract with the state for the old age security pension and that this pension has been increased by the guaranteed income supplement. But one had to
10626

December 20, 1971
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
contribute for ten years before qualifying under the Canada Pension Plan and had to contribute a minimum of five years before receiving even a portion of the moneys so contributed.
One cannot help but agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that perhaps the transfer of moneys places some question on the contract with the state and whether the senior citizens of this country have a right to expect that the old age security pension will continue for many years to come. The hon. member suggested that he is all in favour of a guaranteed annual income, and perhaps this is the final answer. I am also concerned with the suggestion that it would be easier to eliminate the old age security pension if it were funded by payments from the Excise Tax Act into the Consolidated Revenue fund, but I do not think that the guaranteed annual income would be sufficient for many of the senior citizens today. It would pay an equal amount of money to everybody whether or not they were able to earn money and whether or not they had contributed over a long time through sales tax, personal tax and corporation taxes. I remember very well the debate on the Canada Pension Plan. At that time many government members suggested that the old age security pension could be eliminated. I do not think so, and I am suspicious that this might be the first step along that road.
I have other suspicions when looking at this bill, Mr. Speaker. One can wonder how much of the reduction of the tax on television sets, electronic devices and margarine is reflected back to the consumer. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) dealt with this at length but did not get a satisfactory answer. Has the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) and the government looked into this question? Has the price of margarine been reduced? I am inclined to think not, and that the 15 per cent reduction in sales tax on television sets has not been passed on to the consumer. Perhaps the manufacturer in some way is able to absorb this, though I do not think it was intended for his benefit alone but rather to stimulate business through the money being in circulation in one form or another.
I am also suspicious of section 2(2) which reads:
There shall be imposed, levied and collected only six-twelfths of the tax imposed by section 27 on the sale and delivery of the articles enumerated in schedule IV.
In looking at the explanatory notes I believe, and I may be wrong, that this takes the place of the section which provides that there shall be imposed a tax of only three-ninths of the tax imposed by section 27. One does not have to be a mathematical genius to realize that three-ninths is one-third and that six-twelfths is one-half-a substantial increase in the tax levied on articles falling under section 27, schedule IV.
When one looks at schedule IV, section 27 of which deals with a host of implements and farm produce from alfalfa meal, dried or otherwise, to traction engine parts, the increase in the levy is the difference between six-twelfths and three-ninths. The section covers 25 articles. I cannot understand why there is not an explanation for the change from three-ninths to six-twelfths, and I think we must have the answer before much progress is made on

this particular section of the bill. If it is merely a change in the wording, and not in the effect, perhaps the parliamentary secretary or the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) or someone from the government could say so. The parliamentary secretary can hardly speak for the government I suppose, but he is the only one who seems to be paying any attention to what is going on here. The government wonders why its bills do not get speedy passage but they allow the parliamentary secretaries to pilot the bills through in the absence of the ministers.

How much will the treasury lose as a result of the removal of the 15 per cent sales tax on electronic equipment such as television sets, phonograph playing devices and so on? Perhaps the government could also clarify something with regard to the Old Age Security Act. Is this bill the first step towards removing the payment of old age security pensions? People will have to pay for years into the Canada Pension Plan. As soon as people reach pensionable age, they are entitled to draw benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. Will there be some hocus pocus, some playing around with figures and the guaranteed annual income, which will remove benefits that are available to our senior citizens. Is any strategy afoot that will take away these pensions from people who have contributed to them? I hope not.
Remembering what went on when the Canada Pension Plan was introduced, I can only suspect that this bill is the first step towards removing the old age security pension paid to many of our people. Our senior citizens have made major contributions to their pension fund by way of the sales tax. They have contributed 4 per cent of their personal income tax and there have been contributions from corporations in the form of tax. By these means, sizeable contributions have been made to the old age security fund. Our elderly people have a right to expect that, when they reach pensionable age, they will be able to draw benefits from that fund. They expect the state to honour a contract to which it has committed itself. Therefore, any suggestion of this contract being done away with should be squelched immediately.
A long time ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre dealt with this subject at length. He begged the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) to make a
