speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-260, which is before us, is an attempt to put into effect the measures heralded in the mini-budget speech of June 18. That speech was made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). The bill is divided into two sections. One section deals with amendments to the Old Age Security Act and the other removes from the excise tax list certain commodities. The tax reductions indicated in this bill are, generally, welcome. I say that on behalf of members of this party. I will return to the subject in a moment.
First, I should like to spend a few minutes on the section which deals with the amendment to the Old Age Security Act and which removes the 3 per cent of sales tax which has hitherto been earmarked for the old age security fund. That 3 per cent of sales tax revenue is now to be applied to general revenues. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) dealt at some length with his suspicions regarding this particular provision. He went into detail, and I do not intend to go into the same kind of detail in my remarks. I simply want to second what he said. Until the present time, the money necessary for payments under the Old Age Security Act has been
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
collected from three sources: first, from the 4 per cent of personal income tax, the ceiling being $240, which money was paid into the old age security fund; second, from the 3 per cent levy on corporation taxes, which money was paid into the old age security fund; and third, from the 3 per cent of the sales tax levy which, again, was paid into the old age security fund.
We, of this party, have on numerous occasions opposed the regressive nature of two of the sources of income for the old age security fund, namely, the virtually flat rate levied on personal income and the 3 per cent sales tax. We have argued that these taxes were of a regressive nature. Nevertheless, we have always applauded the idea that there ought to be sources of income specially earmarked for payment into the old age security fund, so that it would be patently clear to all concerned that the old age security pension is paid to persons over 65 as of right. They have contributed to the fund during their working years in order to be assured of a pension in their retirement years. The old age security pension is theirs as of right, and the whole matter thus takes on the aspect of a social contract. We have always applauded that fact, even though we may not have approved of certain means used to raise that revenue.
Now, Bill C-259 will remove effectively the 4 per cent of personal income tax that is paid to the old age security fund. That bill will remove the 3 per cent corporation tax contribution which is paid to the same fund. Bill C-260, which we are examining this afternoon, will remove the 3 per cent of sales tax which was formerly paid into the old age security fund. The fund will now be supplied with moneys out of the general revenues, and will receive an income which will be computed on the basis of the taxes that would have been collected if provision for collecting them had still been in effect. That is how the money will be paid and, thus, the contributory nature of the old age security plan will now disappear. As I suggested earlier, the idea of a social contract as between the citizens of this country and the government will also disappear and I am worried, as is the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, about the implications that this move may have for the pensioner. Are we to take it, now that the money for the old age security fund is to come out of the general revenues, that at some future date the government can come to this House and say that since the old age security pension is not a contributory scheme, since it is not a matter of social contract, that it is not paid to pensioners as of right and that the government, therefore, wishes to take that pension away? May I remind the House that one year ago, I believe, the amount of the old age security pension was frozen at $80 per month. That seemed to be the first step to removing the pension entirely. This bill may be the second step. The third step may be taken I do not know when. I hope the government does not intend at some time in the future to end the old age security pension. I hope that some one will get up and tell us that the government does not so intend. The thought that universal pensions may be terminated is very disquieting, and my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre and I are afraid this might happen.
One of the outstanding benefits of the old age security pension was this: it was paid on a demogrant basis. It was paid, as of right, to the senior citizen who had attained a
24725-44!

December 20, 1971
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
certain age. The receipt of that pension was a source of pride. Previous to the Old Age Security Pension becoming universal, a person called himself a pensioner with great reluctance. A pension smacked of welfare. Once it became a demogrant and he contributed to it, it was a source of pride and dignity for the pensioner. Pensioners in this country could organize themselves to come to the government and demand the aid from their fellow citizens which they required and which was their right. They were able to do it on the basis of being pensioners. Their confidence arose from the fact the pension was paid to everyone as a right. If that is to be changed, I suggest it is a retrograde step. If it is to be changed in order to eventually remove the pension paid on a demogrant basis and if all pensioners are going to have to rely on the Canada Pension Plan, private plans and the guaranteed income supplement which is based on a needs test, we have taken a backward step. I hope someone from the government will assure this House that is not their intention and state the philosophy behind these tax changes.
I now turn to the other portion of the bill which deals with the removal of the excise tax from certain commodities. Before dealing with each of the specific items, I wish to make one general statement. In my remarks I will be repeatedly referring to the need for monitoring devices once the tax is removed. I make that demand for two reasons. First, I want to ensure that the benefits of the removal of the tax is passed on to the consumers through reduced prices of goods. The second deals with one of the major problems which every nation has had in managing its economy, that is, attempting to manage the economy through fiscal policies, the manipulation of taxes, which has been largely a by guess and by God operation. No one is ever quite certain what happens when you remove or increase a tax. Here is a real opportunity to do some monitoring and get some hard data about what actually happens when a tax is removed.
These excise taxes were removed effective June 19. We have now had almost six months to monitor the effect of the removal of the taxes to see if the removal did result in added industrial activity, added consumption of goods and more money being put into the economy thereby generating new activity. We have had that occasion presented to us. I hope the government has made use of it. I will be asking the same question again and again when I come to the individual items under these sections of the bill. It is necessary that we undertake such monitoring and collect the hard data about what happens when a tax is removed if we are to effectively use our fiscal policies in the future. I will now deal with the items.
The bill provides for the removal of the excise tax on margarine and similar products. As I indicated in my general remarks, I would like to know whether the removal of the excise tax has been passed on as a saving to the consumer. I received a letter from the Edible Oils Institute in which the Institute extended its thanks to the members of this House for removing the sales tax on edible oils. The Institute gave an undertaking that the saving would be passed on to the consumer. I have no way of knowing that has taken place except by sending my wife out periodically to see whether margarine has gone down in price.
(Mr. Rowland.]
There is available to the government an excellent way of monitoring to see if the removal of the excise tax has actually resulted in savings to the consumer. That way is through the monthly pricing surveys conducted by Statistics Canada. There are large numbers of people employed by Statistics Canada who go to the shopping centres and small grocery stores every month to see what is happening to the prices of various goods. It would take very little effort on the part of the Department of Finance to ask Statistics Canada to make a special effort to price margarine to see whether the saving resulting from the removal of the excise tax is being passed on to the consumer. They could monitor the price of margarine to discover whether the government's fiscal measures have had the desired effect. I would like to know from someone on the government side whether this was done, whether the savings anticipated have indeed been passed on to the consumer or whether they have simply been retained as increased earnings by the companies involved. I mention once again that the Edible Oils Institute assured various members of this House it was their intention to pass on the saving to the consumer. I would like to know if this has been done.
Another section of the bill provides for the removal of excise tax on machinery and products designed for, or related to, the control of pollution. This is a very welcome provision. If the removal of the excise tax does reduce the cost inherent in cleaning up our environment, it is a worthwhile step. I hope it will result in industries, municipalities, the provinces and the federal government being encouraged to purchase the devices necessary to begin cleaning up our environment. Once again, I suggest that, if it has not been done, it is necessary to monitor the effects of the removal of that tax to see that the saving to the companies involved, as the result of the tax being removed, was passed on to the consumer, whether it stimulated the production of anti-pollution devices and whether it stimulated the purchase of domestically produced anti-pollution devices and not simply the importation of anti-pollution devices designed and manufactured abroad. If it has not already been done, those three important aspects should be monitored. I ask whether this has been done and, if so, what were the results of the monitoring?
It would have been useful if the government had come up with a program of research and development in conjunction with this tax measure to ensure that Canadian companies fully benefited from the removal of the excise tax. Such a program would have been another means of ensuring that Canadian companies would undertake research and development into anti-pollution devices to enable them to produce the equipment necessary to clean up our environment and to reduce our dependence on imported goods for this purpose. Had there been a research and development program undertaken in conjunction with the removal of the excise tax, quite possibly we would have had a greater degree of stimulus to that industry than has taken place, if indeed any has taken place. Once again, we will not know precisely what has happened until we have seen the results of the monitoring of the effects of the removal of the tax and we do not know whether that monitoring has taken place.
I would also like to refer to the removal of the excise tax on the electronic equipment such as radios, phonographs
December 20, 1971

and television sets. I come back to the need for monitoring to determine whether that saving has been passed on to the consumer and, being passed on to the consumer, whether that saving has stimulated the purchase of electronic equipment. Also, have the purchases which it has stimulated been of domestic manufacture rather than foreign manufacture. We require these facts, not only to judge the validity of the measures incorporated in this bill, but also to determine the effectiveness of the use of fiscal devices in an attempt to manage our economy.
I said earlier it is largely a by guess and by God operation to attempt to manage the economy through the manipulation of taxes. Monitoring devices would remove some of the elements of doubt from that operation. This was an excellent opportunity to establish monitoring devices. They could have been used to give us some hard information which we require in order to adjust our tax system in the future. As in the case of edible oils, the monitoring in respect of electronic equipment could have been done through Statistics Canada because the pricing of electronic devices takes place monthly in its pricing surveys. A simple request from the Department of Finance could have led to the provision of this information. If such a request has not been made, I suggest the department might approach Statistics Canada and ask for such information to be compiled. It is all there. We could then find out whether the consumer has benefited as a result of these taxation measures.
I have covered, in a sketchy way, most of the subject matter included in the bill. To summarize, there are certain matters in respect to which we should like to be given further information before we vote on this tax bill. First, we should like to know whether our suspicions, as to adjustments in connection with the Old Age Security Act are justified or not. I see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) is in the House. It would be interesting to hear him confirm or deny these suspicions. Second, we should like to know whether the removal of the excise tax from certain commodities have been monitored to determine whether removal has had the results intended, in terms of money saved by consumers, the generation of increased activity in the industry concerned, and increased domestic production, rather than an increase in the importation of manufactured goods.

The fact is that old age pensions, old age security for senior citizens, who

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join other hon. members who have expressed their thoughts on this bill and indicated their approval of these reductions in taxes. Contrary to what the previous speaker has just said, from the speeches I have heard this afternoon hon. members are in favour of doing away with the tax on anti-pollution equipment and the removal of other taxes provided for by the bill. Knowing this bill was to be debated this afternoon, I made some telephone calls to ascertain the facts in connection with the removal of the tax on electronic and television equipment and the tax on margarine. I talked to local people in Ottawa and found, indeed, there had been some price reduction of television sets. The tax reduction has been passed on to some extent.
However, my investigations do not indicate this is the case with the tax on margarine, which I believe was 12 per cent. The same brand of margarine that sold at 59 cents last spring sells today in Ottawa for 66 cents. Even though it may be a loss leader in some stores, and in some of the large chains there may have been large stocks, there should at least have been a maintenance of the price for which it sold before removal of the 12 per cent tax. This indicates to me that the department of the government responsible for implementing the tax reductions should have checked a little more closely, because the removal of the tax has not been reflected in the price of the product. I am sure all hon. members praise the government for removing the tax on anti-pollution equipment; this is a good move. All of us are very conscious of pollution, and before some of the statements made about pollution today become too common in the press some more investigation into pollution is required.
I had an interesting trip to Washington several weeks ago to participate in talks with the United States department of agriculture and other government departments about pollution control. There had been reports in the press that fertilizer used on farmland was causing pollution, and I was interested to note an experiment that had been carried out in this regard in the city of Washington. The experiment disclosed that the major source of pollution from fertilizer was the urban area. Some run-off tests had been made which indicated that urban dwellers, by and large, are ready users of fertilizer which is applied a
December 20, 1971

little more than is generally required on lawns. Some of the chemical is washed off the s.oil and runs down asphalt driveways and pavements into the gutters and thence into streams, and pollution was caused in this way. I think this points to the need for specific investigation as to source of pollution rather than simply referring to pollution generally.
Many speakers this afternoon have referred to the application of the 3 per cent old age security tax to other areas. You can disagree all you like, but what are you and I against the facts? The facts speak much louder than you do in this matter. The facts are that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, along with people who are no longer in this House, carried on a stubborn fight for the old age pensioners. As I say, no one has as much right as he to demand of the parliamentary secretary the reason for these changes. The fact is that not until 1950 did we manage to get the universal old age pension. The battle had been fought step by step since 1924, and only in 1950 was it made a universal old age pension. The contributory feature in it makes it something that can be called a social contract, a contract with society, which gives it a semblance of right. The sweeping away of the contributory factor gives us every reason to feel that the right may be going with it.
It is all very well for my hon. friend sitting straight ahead of me to say that this government has no intention of removing the old age pension. Anybody who knows anything about how liberties are removed knows that very seldom are liberties taken away in a single bite. They are nibbled away. The first approach to the removal of liberty and freedom is not noticed, because it can be explained away as being a more efficient method and as being of benefit to the person who is receiving it. Step by step down the slippery road this continues to happen.
Do not think that some of us over here have forgotten what happened to the universal nature of the old age security pension, or have forgotten that by using fancy language and calling it a guaranteed income supplement the older people in this country were divided into two classes, those who are poor and those who are very poor indeed. The very poor were told that they were benefiting because those a little higher up the income scale did not get a guaranteed income supplement. We have not forgotten that, and we have not forgotten the deprivation of people being kept at a straight $80 a month no matter what happens to the cost of living. These people have no escalator clause, no collective bargaining through which to raise their income in accord with the cost of living. And they were placed in that position by this government. No wonder we are suspicious.
(Mrs. Maclnnis.]
This was done in the smoothest way. The older people were told that they would be regarded as a special category of older people who were self-supporting, and the other people were kept quiet because they were given the so-called guaranteed income supplement and allowed to keep the escalator clause. Their poverty was so desperate that my friends across the way might well have had the revolution referred to by the last government speaker had the older people not been given that kind of sop to keep them quiet.
These are our reasons for wanting an explanation. There are certain rights in this country. The Americans used to refer to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. I will add a fourth right, the right of the old to have self-respect and to be self-respecting. That is a right in this country, or it should be. If this government insists on nibbling away at it with fancy language or with silence, that right will be eroded bit by bit.
We have every right to be given an explanation because there is value in earmarking a fund for the old age security pension. If no particular amount is earmarked for this purpose, every time old age pensions are paid the government will look at the consolidated revenue fund and think that it is a big bite out of the fund and that they had better find some way of chiselling away at it, of putting old age pensioners into another category where they could be given a smaller amount.
If you have a sum of money that you have set aside for a certain purpose and you have effectively said goodbye to that money, you are not tempted to use it for something else. But if you leave that money in a common pot, in your general expense fund, every time you wish to use the money for a special purpose you are tempted to nibble it away and not rob the common pot to that extent. This is why we want a certain amount of money to be set aside by statutory means for the old age security fund, something that cannot be used for another purpose. If suddenly the government tells us that they will take away the sales tax and that it will no longer be put into the old age pension fund, then we have every right to become worried.
At present the old people in this country have been demoted, they do not count any longer. Youth is everything. Once you are over the hill, which is around the age of 30, you are regarded as being of no account. When you get to the stage of receiving the old age pension, somehow this government believes that you are well able to exist on toast and tea and that you enjoy toast and tea more than

I think it would be much more appropriate if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) were to come into the House and tell us exactly why this is being done. After all, this is his bill.
Perhaps I am being a little bolder than my colleagues, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I am going to suggest that from the facts available I already know what is being done. The Minister of Finance has been talking about reducing various taxes through this bill, yet when one looks at the bill it is quite evident that he is increasing the sales tax by 3 per cent. That is exactly what it says. I quote from clause 1:
"27. (1) There shall be imposed, levied and collected a consumption or sales tax of twelve per cent on the sale price of all goods".
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act The act at present in force provides:
There shall be imposed, levied and collected a consumption or sales tax of nine per cent on the sale price of all goods.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, what in my view and in the opinion of the Carter commission on taxation is a very regressive form of taxation is being increased by 3 per cent through this bill. That is what it says. There is a later clause in the bill which abolishes certain provisions of the Old Age Security Act. That, to me, is a purely incidental piece of legislation because in effect it abolishes the 3 per cent contribution to the old age security fund. But it is quite apparent, on the face of the facts of the legislation, that what is being done is to reduce the amount of money going into the old age security fund and on the other hand to permanently increase the sales tax by 3 per cent.
Hon. members may recall that the Carter commission report said if there was going to be a sales tax at all-and it said sales tax should continue-then sales tax both federal and provincial should be levied at the retail level, rather than continuing in our tax law this particularly iniquitous form of taxation that bears most heavily on the consumer and is one of the factors contributing to inflation.
If one compares this bill with Bill C-259 this was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-he will see there is no parallel provision in regard to sales tax as there is in regard to income tax. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre remarked earlier, that legislation points out that an amount equal to the amount that might have been collected from income tax, under the direct 3 per cent and 4 per cent contributions from corporations and personal income tax, shall be put into the fund by the Minister of National Revenue. There is nothing in this bill which says that shall be done with the extra 3 per cent sales tax to be levied. It is quite clear to me what the government has in mind. It is going to rob the old age security fund of the 3 per cent that is now going into it and put that money into general revenues. The practical effect in the long run will be an increase of 3 per cent in this regressive form of taxation to be used for the general spending programs of the government.
The hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) said there would be a revolution if the government were to tamper with this. But some of us recall the kind of suggestions that came from government and near-government sources during the period prior to the tabling of the white paper with the blue cover, called "Income for Canadians", by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). And some of us recall the relief and surprise-certainly pleasure so far as I was concerned-that was felt when he indicated in that white paper that for the time being at least the universal old age security pension was to be continued.
As I say, there had been widespread suggestions emanating from government and near-government sources that the universal old age pension plan might be changed. Now I am beginning to feel that in the internal discussions of the government this philosophy is winning out and this bill is a symbol and a sample of it. If one couples this with the earlier action mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway regarding the freezing of the old age security pension at $80, this at a time when because of cost of living increases obviously a substantial increase

I suggest it is the Minister of Finance, rather than the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who should come into this House and tell us whether or not that is happening with respect to the direction of government policy at this time. The president of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities communicated to the Minister of Finance the concern of municipalities regarding a particular aspect of the budget and tax reform proposals submitted on June 18, 1971. The Minister of Finance wrote to the federation and in an attempt to answer their concern said:
To further encourage the acquisition of anti-pollution equipment, I wish to announce the immediate withdrawal of the sales tax on such equipment used in production. This new exemption will apply to all machinery and apparatus which manufacturers or producers acquire to detect, prevent, remove or reduce pollutants of water, soil or air. The exemption will reduce revenues by about $8 million a year.
The letter, dated June 18, 1971, was sent from the House of Commons and bears the signature of the Minister of Finance. That is the type of correspondence that the federation is concerned about, because apparently little consideration is being given to extending the same advantages to municipalities as are to be extended to manufacturers. A news release dated December 17, 1971, and put out by the Department of the Environment says, in part:
Environment Canada will take the lead among federal departments in elimination of pollution by government installations across Canada.
Since departments of the federal government are prepared to take the lead in eliminating pollution, and since the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has asked for the same privileges that are to be extended to manufacturers, I suggest that for not being prepared to assist municipalities across Canada in this regard the government stands condemned.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: Right.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
This area needs consideration. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance is prepared to give favourable consideration to the requests of the municipalities. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture, who should also be concerned about pollution control measures, will come to realize that the municipalities are the foundation of our society and that their needs should be considered. It is fine and dandy to say that federal

government departments will be active in the area of pollution control. The basic unit of our society is the municipality. In common with manufacturers and producers, municipalities hope that they will be given blanket exemption from federal sales tax on the purchase of antipollution equipment.
No doubt many hon. members in this House have served on municipal councils. Others who have not so served have been associated with people active in municipalities and local communities. At present it appears that the federal government is not prepared-hopefully, I am wrong-to revise its schedule of exemptions and include municipalities as entities eligible for exemptions with regard to anti-pollution equipment. One must ask, exactly what is the government trying to do to the small municipalities across this country?
We have heard many times about pollution control measures, sewage disposal plants and all the rest that will assist in controlling pollution. At the same time the government has introduced Bill C-260 which does not provide pollution control measures or the machinery connected with those measures as far as municipalities are concerned. Surely this government is not insensitive to the concern of the municipalities. They must realize that municipalities need concessions along the same lines as those which manufacturers are receiving. Surely the submission made by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities bears considerable weight.
I look forward to questions being asked when this bill is before committee of the whole, so that we will hear the real reason for the government not including municipalities. I hope that responsible ministers of the government will be present and these questions will be answered in committee. These ministers, speaking for their departments, can tell the people of Canada that they will provide concessions along the lines to which I referred, similar to those granted manufacturers and producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate this evening. While I realize we are approaching the festive season, there is no reason why it should become a silly season. It has come close to being that. I found the speeches of members opposite almost incredible. I did not hear a word about the removal of sales tax on margarine. I wonder why. That is probably the most important feature.
Bill C-260 is a relatively insignificant bill, yet the members of the New Democratic Party are making speech after speech. I have been asking myself why they are doing this. What are they going to do? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), an experienced and able parliamentarian, spoke in the House this afternoon. He attempted to establish a link with the 1950 report of the Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on Old Age Security. He waved a blue document before us. I am familiar with that report. I worked for several years as a public servant in the Department of National Health and Welfare. We used that important document.
December 20, 1971

What was the link? The link was the great virtue of having a contributory pension plan. The report of the Senate and House of Commons committee included in its recommendations a contributory pension plan, the 3-3-3 formula. It was originally 2-2-2 but was later changed to 3-3-3, corporation income, personal income and sales tax. I can understand the hon. member talking about the psychological link between the individual's contribution of income tax and pension. The continuous link, which the member spent his entire speech trying to establish, was that putting 3 per cent earmarked from the sales tax into a fund was an absolutely necessary element of a pension scheme.
I have heard ridiculous speeches, statements and propositions before but in the period in which I have been a member of this House, never anything to quite equal that. To suggest that somehow part of a sales tax, when put into a fund, makes it a little more virtuous, conspicuous and does something for the great integrity of the individual is something that I never expected to hear from a responsible member of the House of Commons, especially the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
If we want to talk about contributory pensions, I can understand the point that has to be made in the proper scheme of things. But let us do it in a reasonable and sensible way. Let us not have speech after speech demanding that the minister say whether he is going to abolish the old age security program. That is complete and utter nonsense from serious members on the other side.
I keep asking myself "Why these speeches? Why this nonsense? Why this drivel?" I say it is drivel coming from members opposite who normally make good speeches. In this instance they are far wide of the mark in refusing to deal with the merits of a relatively insignificant piece of legislation. The legislation removes the sales tax on margarine, television sets and other electronic apparatus and amends the old age security financing formula to make sure that the sales tax portion is no longer labelled the way it was. It does not affect the incidence or the level of sales tax.
I suggest their purpose is to consume the time of the House to avoid a discussion on other legislation. They are wasting the time of the House. But the people of Canada, the taxpayers and the voters, have a right to recognize what hon. members opposite, those of the NDP bearing smiles on their faces, have done here this afternoon and are doing tonight.

Frankly, I am not one who is particularly involved in the question of sales tax. I am one who believes that a sales tax is a retrograde tax, a tax that must be paid by those who cannot really afford to do so and by those who can afford to do so, indiscriminately. Most governments have used it as an emergency measure to raise revenue but, unfortunately, it always seems to become permanent. The tax we are considering has not changed. It was levied at the rate of 11 per cent or 12 per cent, and under this bill it will continue to be 11 per cent or 12 per cent. Most people who advocate tax reform do not really approve of it as a long-term tax.
I differ from some of the statements made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), but I agree with him that this bill is concerned with only a small portion of the sales tax which has been directed to old age security. Originally, in 1952, this money was raised in three ways and a good deal of consideration was given to whether or not part of the tax should be in the form of a sales tax. At that time, personal income tax accounted for 2 per cent, corporation tax for another 2 per cent and the sales tax for a further 2 per cent. As I recall it, there was a $60 maximum on personal tax contributions. This situation changed over the years. It went to three, three and three. Then for several years the tax was 4 per cent on personal income, 3 per cent on corporation income and 3 per cent on sales tax. I do not know whether many members realize that we have eliminated the 4 per cent personal contribution and the 3 per cent collected from the corporations. The hon. member for Ottawa West may have known.
I listened to much of the debate which took place on Bill C-259. I was lucky to keep up with discussions as they were going on. I never claimed I had spent my summer reading this bill and becoming totally familiar with it. I can honestly say that I was not personally aware that the old age security fund was to be eliminated as a contributo-

ry fund. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) shakes his head. I give him credit for having studied this bill. It pays him a little money to study this bill. I will say frankly that he has earned that money. He is one of the few parliamentary secretaries who has. I have always been impressed by the attitude taken by many Conservatives and, indeed, by some of the older members of the New Democratic Party as well as by some of the older Liberals; they would not accept old age security pension if they thought it was a gift from the treasury. They were always told, and they believed, that they received a pension as of right because they had contributed toward it.
Since 1952, almost 20 years ago, they have made regular contributions of between $60 and $120 to a fund from which they could draw a pension as of right because they had contributed to it. There are thousands of people in this country who will not apply for an old age supplementary benefit simply because it is a hand-out from the government, and because to receive it they must show they are destitute. I am sure not many people in this House would say they do not know many older people in their constituencies who would not accept welfare, who would not accept a dole but who would accept the old age pension. It is a dishonest government, it is a dishonest Minister of Health (Mr. Munro) and a dishonest Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson)-

speechtext: I would ask the hon. member whether the suggestion that the amount of the old age pension be mentioned on the tax form or included in the basic rate is not merely a question of semantics or a technical point. speechtext:
That is not what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said. He said the principle of universality should be carried on. The minister has stated everyone would be entitled to a certain payment out of the fund. The only problem arises when the amount has to be increased. The government made an additional payment which it called a supplement, but applied a means test. But in both the government's white paper and the report on social services the case for universality is made. Family allowances, and I suggest old age security as well from now on, will drop the principle of universality and the government will only pay out when there is a need.
As far as unemployment insurance is concerned, all workers are going to contribute, but only a few will ever get money from the fund. But my point is that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) did not tell us, or if he did I did not understand him, that the government was going to eliminate the contributory section from the old age security legislation and that the money would be paid out of a general fund. However, the government has not yet been able to design a scheme of income tax to get this money back again, though my colleague for Winnipeg North Centre hit upon an ingenious idea that eliminated most of the tax at the bottom end yet offered the same exemptions all the way up.
I suppose you would soon reach a Utopian system where everybody would be paid all kinds of dividends, or whatever you might care to call them, and only those who would need them would keep them. That is not what we are talking about when we speak about a guaranteed annual wage and a negative income tax structure. We believe that everybody has the right to at least a reasonable amount of money.
We believe that the tax structure should be such that when money is not needed it is returned to the state, so
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
that if a demogrant is given to an old age pensioner who has $5 million or $6 million, he is entitled to it but obviously some of that money should come back to the state. Obviously when a demogrant is not needed, the money should be returned to the state. However, the government is obviously making a change in the whole field. They are telling the public that this is a just society in which a just amount would be given to those at the bottom of the scale, and going all the way up the scale.
This government was faced recently with a court action and was told in effect that the law must be obeyed in the same way by everyone. If the law says you must pay out money, then you must pay it out. I presume that so long as the old age security fund exists, the government has the obligation to pay out at least the basic old age security to everyone who has made a contribution to that fund. Of course, there are limits and exceptions depending on how long you have lived in the country and a number of other factors, but that was your money and you had a right to it.
I suppose that someone in the legal department said that if that fund is established it would have to be used for that purpose. However, if we wipe out the fund and we decide to pay the demogrant-and I agree that there has been no indication from the government that they will not pay it-of $80 to old age pension recipients, they will not receive less money. Nevertheless, if the old age pensioner decides that that is a hand-out, that that is money he has not earned and is not entitled to, then I suggest he will consider and I will consider that the system has been changed. There is nothing we can do about it. But I think that everybody in this country owes a great deal of gratitude to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who has brought this to our attention.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: You must be kidding.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is one of those who believes, as do many Liberals, that so long as someone receives the money, it does not matter where it comes from. One can belong to the high church in the better part of the town, rent quarters in the slums at an exorbitant rent to poor tenants who cannot do anything about it, but the money is clean. This is like the Mafia. In my opinion it is very important where the money comes from and by what means it comes.
There is a great difference between receiving money from the Canada Pension Plan and receiving it from someone else because I do not have enough money to feed my wife and keep a roof over our heads. Every time I crawl to some civil servant who is a welfare officer I will certainly' be made well aware of the difference between that money and the money which I receive in my own right and to which I have contributed. People who have not had to do without do not see the difference. The landlord who never goes to the slums does not feel bad. They hire people to go to the slums and to evict other people; they do not do it themselves. It is not dirty business because they do not come into contact with it. But in my opinion there is a considerable difference between that money and the money one gets as one's right. I hope that eventually the government will bring Parliament and the country up to date on their thoughts regarding the old age pension. They will have to do that so far as programs like the old age pension are concerned.

December 20, 1971
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: "Is" concerned.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: I have already indicated that we come from different sides of the track. The point I want to make for the people on my side of the track-

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext: And there are more of them.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
-is that they have a right to know what their future will be in terms of social security. This reminds me very much of a fellow getting a job in some of the industries in which I have worked, such as a mine which closes down after 19 years. It closes down just as the old age security fund is closing down. After 19 years your are out of a job, there is no money left in the fund, you do not have a pension-in those days pension plans were not portable-and you have to start all over again. You hope that the next job you get will be better.
I think the people have the right to know where Canada is going in terms of social security. They have the right to know why it is advantageous to drop the contributions to this fund. This was the first major piece of social security in this country. It was a fund which the government did not find obnoxious to administer. The money was not invested in some agencies. I am in agreement with those members who say that we should continue to pay the demogrant at the present time. However, I wonder why we wiped it out. Obviously, there must be a reason why the 4 per cent was wiped out.
I would have made some changes to that fund. I would have taken off the ceiling and I would have allowed enough money to accumulate in the old age security fund to allow us to pay greatly increased benefits to the older people of this country. There were a number of changes that could have been made. But I cannot see the reason for eliminating the old age security fund. Obviously, this is done for a purpose. My suggestion is that the government is eliminating it so as to change the whole idea of the demogrant and from now on more and more of our basic social legislation will be based on a means test.
This government will say to the people, "You have to establish a need no matter what kind of grant you get. We will not pay the old age security pension to people who are not in need, but we will pay more than $80, perhaps even more than $130 to people who will establish need." This does not answer the question which the older people of Canada will have to ask themselves concerning the removal of the sense of integrity which people feel they had under the old age security plan and which they now have with the Canada Pension Plan because they make contributions to it. They have put money into it. They have contributed in whatever way the government wanted them to contribute to the fund. It is their fund. They want to enjoy that fund as a right.
It seems to me the government has not done any good service by removing surreptitiously, through Bill C-259, the 4 per cent personal contribution and the 3 per cent corporation share, and now through Bill C-260 removing the sales tax as a contribution to the old age pension fund. This will not make people richer.
One hon. member said that the sales tax has been removed from oleomargarine and from some dairy

spreads. That is a slippery move, as one of my colleagues says. I suppose the extent of its slipperiness depends upon whether you are a farmer or not. And the government has removed the tax from pollution control machinery. Municipalities have had to fight pollution, and in fact they have been large-scale sources of pollution themselves. It is good that the tax is removed in that respect. The government lends municipalities money to fight pollution. I believe it should provide municipalities with the necessary machinery at as low a cost as possible. If necessary it should undertake the manufacture of pollution control machinery itself, and give such machinery to municipalities.
If the bill did not contain this provision I am quite sure it would have passed without much debate. But I am certain that anyone who listened to the speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre must now be concerned. He pointed to the loss of something that most of us have grown fond of, the old age security program. Mr. Speaker, some of our own members are taking advantage of that program. An increase in salary does not prevent one from taking advantage of it.
As I say, most of us support the idea of an old age security pension fund built up in part by contributions from individuals and in part by contributions from corporations. Collecting such contributions through sales tax has worked well. We are unhappy that the pension will now be regarded as a government hand-out, rather than something to which pension recipients themselves contributed.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND OLD AGE SECURITY ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the surface, what we are being asked to do through changing the source of this tax simply looks like an administrative matter to clean things up. But we have a duty to look beyond what appears on the surface and examine the full implications of such a move. I am concerned that something which may be of great importance to the future of the old age pension scheme is being put through in the dying hours of this session. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has sometimes been called the conscience of Parliament. As that conscience he is very much concerned about old age pensioners. There is no one in this country who has fought so well for old age pensioners as the hon. member, and he is to be excused if he wants to know what will happen with this kind of legislation.
This debate illustrates a fundamental difference between some of us on this side of the House and other hon. members. This difference is between looking upon some government activity in the redistribution of income as a form of charity, or as a matter of right. There is an important principle involved. We in this party have always argued that in seeking redistribution of income we should get people to look after their own needs by contributing to government programs. In short, we saw the state in competition with private insurance plans and felt the state could introduce far better insurance programs- fairer, more equitable, cheaper to administer, and providing more benefits to all-and we believed in public involvement in those programs.
One of the schemes for which we fought and in which we believe strongly is the old age security pension pro-
December 20, 1971

gram. It is not a charity, not something to be buried in the general tax structure. It is a program that should be highly visible. People should see that they themselves are contributing to it, and when they collect their pension they should know the pension is theirs as a matter of right and not a charitable gesture.
We have much reason to be suspicious of what the government has been doing to universal programs recently. For example, the old age pension has been frozen at $80. It seems inconceivable that a large group of people will never receive any increase in their old age pension and that in future increments are to be based on a means test. The government can call this test whatever it wants, but it winds up being a means test. We believe it is grossly unfair.
We have argued that this discriminates against people who have small savings or a small pension from another source. Some of the predictions we made about the difficulties created by the introduction of such a means test have become realities. More and more old age pensioners are becoming resentful that the small amounts they earn from baby sitting or other sources disqualifies them from increases in their old age pensions. They feel cheated, betrayed and let down by the people who administer the program.
The government is taking the same approach to family allowances. On a number of occasions the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) has said he intends to revamp the whole family allowances program. I will not deal with that question in this debate, but it indicates the direction in which the government is moving. It is trying to drop universal programs or turn them into programs that contain some kind of means test.
We are not opposed to increases being given to those in need. This is a cornerstone of our policy. But it seems to us that the additional resources needed to do this are not coming from those who have the ability to pay. They are not coming from industries like oil and gas which pays minimal tax. They are not coming from people who make their living from capital gains. The necessary tax is coming from those who can least afford to pay it. The redistribution is not from the well-to-do to the poor; it is from the near-poor to the poor. This is not a good way to redistribute wealth. If the old age pension is frozen at a low level and the same happens to family allowances, then it is the near-poor who are hurt.
We cannot give our approval to a program that abandons universality and moves toward the introduction of a means test, particularly when the necessary tax is being levied on those who can ill afford to pay it and when benefits are being taken away from people who are entitled to them by virtue of their contributions to the program.
One of the things that sets Canada apart is the intelligent use made up to now of both the old age pension and the family allowance. This makes us different from our neighbours to the south in terms of our social outlook and how we view justice as between people. I am very unhappy to see anything introduced that would work against such programs. If there is an advantage to the sales tax and to part of it going to pay for the old age pension, it is
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
the argument that the program is not universal in its contributory form because the poor who collect it do not pay income tax or corporation tax. But everyone pays sales tax in some form, and everyone who collects the old age pension, even if they never file an income tax return, has in fact contributed because of the sales tax on their purchases over the years.
While most of us regard sales tax as regressive and have been looking for ways out of it, there is a realization that it is going to become a larger instrument of government revenues than it is at present. It has been the experience of many European countries that a tax on consumables, including the necessities of life but also at other levels, is a cheap way of raising taxes. By allocating a portion of the sales tax to the old age pension fund we can guarantee that it will increase and continue to serve old age pensioners in the future, but by trying for administrative ease the government will destroy the philosophical basis and the justification for a separate fund for old age pensions. I for one, Mr. Speaker, think that the government owes this House an explanation of its intentions and its reasons for wanting these particular changes made now. If we do not get an explanation then we must suspect that the government has other things in mind than trying to make things easy for civil servants.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in the debate on this very interesting bill. First, I must say that the changes dealing with the Old Age Security Act make one wonder where we are going. Therefore I look forward to hearing the real reasons behind the proposed changes.
I should like to speak briefly on those sections of the bill dealing with anti-pollution equipment. Our group has been pressing for the exemption of anti-pollution equipment from the sales tax as one of the incentives to encourage all groups in Canada to take a more active role in pollution abatement. The municipalities need the most assistance, but as I read the bill they are not covered by the exemptions in it. I feel that this matter should be of interest to every member of the House. Municipal groups have come to us from one end of Canada to the other asking for tax relief.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) asked the parliamentary secretary whether municipalities were covered in the exemptions, but to date we have not received the information. From the material we have received from the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities it is my impression that the municipalities are not covered. I ask the parliamentary secretary and all members of this House, why should we give industry exemption from sales tax on anti-pollution equipment and not give it to municipalities which in my opinion need it most? This is one of the reasons we are interested in discussing the bill on second reading.
I wish to tell the parliamentary secretary through you, Mr. Speaker, that if they do not bring in an amendment to clause 4 giving some relief to municipalities on sales tax respecting anti-pollution equipment, we will bring in an amendment and have another debate on it. This is the very thing we have been preaching and urging. Groups have been appearing before our committees for months asking for some kind of relief, yet Bill C-260 does not

cover the municipalities of Canada. Why is the exemption given only to industry? I think clause 4(2)(b) is the key to the whole thing. It provides:
machinery and apparatus sold to or imported by manufacturers or producers for use by them directly in the detection, measurement, prevention, treatment, reduction or removal of pollutants to water, soil or air attributable to the manufacture or production of goods-
There are other clauses which can be dealt with in committee. The municipalities in many instances do not have the tax base to allow them to take adequate measures for control, and I see absolutely no reason why they are not included in this legislation. I should like to refer again to the news release issued by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities on September 21, 1971. speechtext:
I am not saying that, because there is no question here of an individual contributing amounts which will be equivalent in any way to his pension. After all, the person who is well-to-do contributes a great deal more than the pension he will receive. I was talking about the feeling of participation.
That point was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and many others. He and others talking about this sense of participation. You can see it under the Canada Pension Plan. The idea of participation is reinforced by the Canada Pension Plan, and it seems to me it is a good idea for the individual to identify the payments he makes as being contributions toward the old age security pension. If we ever come to the point of the guaranteed annual income, either by introducing the negative income tax or tax credits-and I always thought that Bill C-259 was wrong because it did not use the tax credit system-we will need to organize the income tax on a much more flexible basis if we are to take care of aspects of that kind. Some provinces are ready to move in that direction. However, we are opening up a much wider field for discussion than is contemplated by this clause.
As I understand it, tariff item 47600-1 deals with certain equipment. I am referring to the items listed under subparagraph (3). Tariff item 47815-1 deals primarily with surgical equipment and with driving kits that persons who are incapacitated because of physical infirmity may fit to their automobiles so that they may drive them. That is perfectly all right and I entirely support this provision.
There is one point that I should like to see developed more, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Kootenay West discussed it with some vehemence a short while ago and I wish to deal with it. I felt that removing the sales tax as an incentive for manufacturers to purchase anti-pollution equipment was a step in the right direction. In other words, manufacturers can now acquire such equipment without paying tax. The scope of this measure is very limited. According to clause 4, section 20 (2) (b) found on page 2 of the bill, such machinery and apparatus must be used directly in the detection, measurement, prevention, treatment, reduction or removal of pollutants to water, soil or air attributable to the manufacture or production of goods.
I think this provision may be fairly limited. I am not sure how far these people will be able to move. The hon. member for Kootenay West said that the provision should be given to municipalities, but the municipalities in the main are not in the business of producing goods. I think under the National Housing Act, and I would certainly like to see the government move in this direction, the credits could be improved and upgraded.
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
Rather than a sales tax credit, municipalities could be given an incentive for forgiveness features in loans for sewage treatment plants in the secondary and tertiary fields. This is a much better program than saying to the municipalities or provincial governments that they can take off the sales tax. There is a difficulty with the provinces. The federal and provincial governments have agreements whereby they each pay the sales tax to the other chap. If you start making exceptions, you get into difficulty. I do not think that is the way to approach it.
With regard to municipalities and provinces in connection with machinery, equipment and installations to deal with pollution control, it is far better to have a major incentive scheme of the kind that existed. Some may still exist although they are very limited. These provide forgiveness features on loans for programs with regard to these very expensive control systems. There are no two ways about it, they are very expensive. That is the only way that can be done. To say that municipalities and provinces should not have to pay sales tax on machinery or apparatus used in the production of goods is not feasible. It is another thing to put it in a category where you can undertake a major program that will bring results across the whole country, not just on a hit-or-miss basis as it might be.
I sympathize with the objective of inducing municipalities and provinces to enter the field of pollution control, but with the greatest of respect I do not think this is the place to do it. If I were in support of the idea of introducing an amendment, I might find some difficulty in limiting it within the terms of the ways and means motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the explanatory notes to this bill make clear, clause 1 is consequential to clause 5. I mention that as a prelude to making the statement that I think we should be entitled to discuss clauses 1 and 5 together since their combined effect is one operation, namely, the removal of the 3 per cent sales tax from the Old Age Security Act and the adding of 3 percentage points to the sales tax set out in the Excise Tax Act. As hon. members are aware, this area has concerned many of us who have taken part in this debate. We have done so because of a very real concern as to what use might be made of this change of tax policy in the future.
I say to the hon. member for Ottawa West that I listened with interest to his criticism earlier in this debate. However, I submit that there is one thing one has to watch around this place. That is the danger that victories that were won can be lost. As a matter of fact, I was quoting this afternoon from the report of the special joint committee on old age security that met in 1950. I remind any who were around at that time and those who have read history that one of the prominent members of that committee was David Croll, now a member of the other place. He was not only a prominent member of the joint committee, being then a member of the House of Commons, but he was one of the hardest fighters for the complete removal of the means test and for establishing old age security on a universal basis.
That same David Croll is now the chairman of a committee which recently issued a report stating, among other things, that the Old Age Security Act should be abolished,

December 20, 1971
Excise Tax Act and Old Age Security Act
this proposal having been made in the context of his particular plan for a guaranteed annual income. I am simply making the point that things that were once won, and which one thought might have been established, can be lost if one does not watch out.
I expressed my fear this afternoon and I express it again tonight. By removing the direct relationship between individuals and the whole concept of old age security through the way in which they pay their taxes, there can be a lessening of the declared right to old age security on a universal basis. I again point out that one not only has material from as far back as 1950, but there is the white paper of the present Minister of National Health and Welfare which was tabled only a year ago. In it the minister said, among other things:
Personal income taxes as well as other earmarked taxes have been collected from people since 1952 to finance this program, establishing an expectation and a right to the pension.
The point I am trying to make is that this government has said time and again that one of the reasons that justifies the universality of the old age pension is that people pay for it through taxes that are identified for old age security. My fear is that if there is no such relationship, this or some succeeding government may go still further in terms of whittling away the universality that we wrote into the Old Age Security Act.
I remember a prominent deputy minister of welfare saying in a public address a few years ago that one of the real sources of pride in this country is the fact that we have established family allowances and old age pensions on a universal basis, and with this sort of thing having been won we can count on it being here for all time. That is not the case. That is my concern about this change in the tax basis.
At no time this afternoon did I or anyone else in this group suggest that this change envisages doing away with old age pensions. What it does envisage is the possibility of arguing against the universal right which has been related to the earmarked taxes. That is what I would like to fend off. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, if we can now get the Minister of Finance to make a statement on this matter, it will be extremely welcome. He may have his reasons for not having referred to it in his budget speech of June 18, or when he introduced Bill C-259, or when this bill was introduced today.
We were told about these changes in respect of all three taxes in the resolutions and in the bills, but not one word has been said in explanation. But if the minister can now tell us that there is a philosophy behind this, that there is a rationale, and that it is not the intention of the government in the course of these changes in tax policy as far as old age pensions are concerned, to cut by one iota the right to universal pensions, I shall be pleased. I may even be satisfied.
But before he does that, may I correct one thing 1 said this afternoon and which I have since found to be wrong. Let me be the first to correct it. It was drawn to my attention by someone else, but I am happy to correct it. I made the statement this afternoon that the Minister of National Revenue would in the future be required to estimate the amount which^ would have been collected in

personal old age security tax and in corporation old age security tax and that this amount would have to be transferred from the consolidated revenue fund into the old age security fund. Along with that I said this was not to be done with respect to sales tax. I now find that under the wording of Bill C-259 cross-related to section 24 of the Old Age Security Act the same thing would happen with respect to sales tax revenues.
Thus, an amount estimated to be what would have been derived had the old law still been in effect would be transferred to the fund. In other words, it is clear there is to be no change, in the immediate future at any rate, in the total amount of dollars going over. But this does not detract from the basic point we have made this afternoon, namely, that the earmarked relationship, the sense individuals have that they are paying for old age security and are therefore entitled to it, is to be wiped out by the way in which this is being done.
The Minister of Finance will probably tell us that the old age security fund as such is being retained. This, I might say, is a bit of fiction. It is just a matter of bookkeeping. I think that what is more important is to retain something which emphasizes each individual's right to a pension because of his contribution in one or two or three ways. I come back again to the report the committee made in 1950 and which the government accepted in 1951, namely, that it was a good idea to have this kind of relationship. I would not like to see it go, because the danger is created of the possibility that the government could get away from the universal concept, as has already happened in connection with the guaranteed income supplement. We have seen it happen, too, with respect to family allowances.
One of the reasons I am not unreservedly supporting the hon. member for Humber-St.-George's-St. Barbe in his frequent requests that the bill which deals with family security be enacted right away, is that although provision is made for improvement in the allowances to be paid it is accompanied by income tests which I think ought to be looked at very closely. This is my concern in connection with the legislation before us. I say to the hon. member for Ottawa West, despite his fun this evening, that it is a real concern. When I saw that this earmarked tax relationship, declared to be a prop for universality, was being removed, I was most concerned about what might happen in the future.
I hope that this debate, if it does nothing else, will produce a statement on what I suggest is an important subject and one on which we have heard not one word thus far from the Minister of Finance.

speechtext:
I should like to say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there is no intention to get rid of the universality of the basic old age pension. The government has often indicated this to be the situation.
When we were going through the process of reviewing personal and corporate income tax in connection with Bill C-259, one of the stated intentions was to get rid of designated taxes such as the old age security tax, the social development tax, and so on, and combine them in one system. At the same time, we did not want to get rid of the old age security fund. So what we have done in the bill before us, which takes care of the sales tax as well, is this:
December 20, 1971

we have authorized the Minister of National Revenue to transfer to the fund personal income tax, corporate income tax and sales tax in an amount equivalent to what would have been derived from the various percentages applied as special taxes. I believe this is a more efficient way of doing things. It makes it a little simpler for people to calculate their personal tax, and I think this is desirable.
As to people knowing that they contribute to the old age security fund, I doubt whether the majority of people even know they pay the sales tax, let alone that a certain percentage goes to the fund. The fund is to continue. There is no desire to get rid of universality. I think I have given the hon. member the assurance for which he is asking.

Before I am through, Mr. Chairman, I will be making this afternoon's speech all over again. I pointed out this afternoon that old age security is not based on each individual's account. This is the way we recommended in 1950 and I accept that way. If my hon. friend reads about this matter in the white paper entitled "Income Security for Canadians" he will find the idea is expressed that old age security which is financed without individual accounts is the first deck of a total social security program. I approve of this arrangement whereby the first deck is financed without individual accounts but in a way that the people feel they have a right to the money.
Then the second deck, the Canada Pension Plan, is on an individual account or contributory basis. I think that these two together make a pretty good program. I do not want to see them destroyed by a government that nibbles away at the first deck, namely, universal old age security.

Mr. Chairman, I am still not convinced by the Minister of Finance of the advisability of retaining an account. Personally, I see little merit in it. I presume the minister issues these cheques out of general treasury and I cannot see any point in keeping money in the general treasury that is used for a specific purpose. If this country goes broke we just are not going to pay our old age pensioners their cheques; it is that simple.
The old system was based on a totally different concept. I know we are eliminating it, but my point is that I do not see the merit of retaining the money in a specific account. Previously the 3 per cent sales tax went specifically into this fund. Now it will not. The 12 per cent tax will be paid into the federal treasury and the Receiver General will turn the money over to the Minister of National Health and Welfare who will issue the cheques, but I do not think that this meets the point about the rights of individuals who have made contributions. I suppose that the 4 per cent on my income tax, which will of course be handled by the Minister of National Revenue in a somewhat different way, will not cost me any the less though I shall not be paying 4 per cent as such.
If I may talk on clause 1, I shall not talk on the other clauses. I should like to make a general plea to the minister. There are some people in this country who cannot speak very well for themselves but who nevertheless have a personal interest in these matters. One of these groups is that which receives old age security, and another is the group which receives family allowance. I think there

I do not discount in this the unemployment insurance legislation, though the payments are being treated in almost the same way but on a means test.
