maintopic: AGRICULTURE-PROGRAM TO ASSIST SMALL FARMERS- NATURE OF PLAN-ADJUSTMENT FOR SIMILAR PROVINCIAL PROJECTS
AGRICULTURE-PROGRAM TO ASSIST SMALL FARMERS- NATURE OF PLAN-ADJUSTMENT FOR SIMILAR PROVINCIAL PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to address the House this evening because of the very insufficient answer I received from the Parliamentary Secretary to the minister of Agriculture (Mr. Lessard) pertaining to the question of whether or not the House of Commons will have the opportunity to debate the government's program to supposedly aid small farmers in their attempts to expand their operations.
The answer I received is indicative of the negative attitude of this government to agriculture. Its performance in the last four years has been anything but good. To appreciate this hon. members need only look at the Lift program which proved to be a disaster, at the inadequacy of the stabilization program and the mess in which we find ourselves with regard to Bill C-176. It seems that the government is reluctant to discuss the merits or demerits of its program for small farmers. What is the definition of a small farmer in terms of the program? Is the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) suggesting that he does not know?
If this government is really serious about aiding the small farmers in Canada, then it must create a viable agricultural economy that will show the small farmer that it is worth while for him to go further into debt in order to develop a sound economic unit.
There are two very important problems facing the farmers in Canada which the government must be prepared to tackle. First is the very low returns the farmer is getting for his products. Farmers are receiving only the same price, if not less, for their products as they were receiving decades ago. Therefore, the government should bring in a two-price system for wheat. The domestic price should be $1.25 a bushel more than the bushel being sold on the international market. This would mean an additional $70 million approximately for the producer, while the cost to the consumer would be minimal. After all, we on the Prairies have heard the Liberal party promise a two-price
December 20, 1971

system for seven long years. It is time they introduced one.
In view of the rising costs of production the government should be prepared to bring in a price support program for other grains as well. This brings me to the second area of concern to farmers, the accelerating costs of production. The government spent thousands of dollars on the Barber Royal Commission on the Price of Farm Machinery to tell every farmer what he knows, namely, that the price of farm machinery is too high. It is time the government seriously examined the farm machinery industry in order to find means of curtailing the ever-rising costs which the farmer has to face.
In conclusion, if the government wants to encourage the small farmers to stay in the business of farming, it must come to grips with the cost-price squeeze in which the farmer finds himself.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Lessard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-PROGRAM TO ASSIST SMALL FARMERS- NATURE OF PLAN-ADJUSTMENT FOR SIMILAR PROVINCIAL PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not very easy to reply to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) because the hon. gentleman asked me to define a small farm. Depending on the type of production in which a farmer is engaged, it might involve quite different implications. To decide tonight on a precise definition of a small farm is not possible. It is doubtful if debate on such a definition at this time would be a useful exercise, for at this stage it is to a large degree variable. This is one of the reasons for embarking on this endeavour as a program rather than as specific legislation. The government recognizes the complexity of the problem and prefers to obtain some experience in this field prior to introducing legislation.
The minister indicated on another occasion that funds for this program have been voted upon and approved by the House in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the past two fiscal years. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member would not wish to dispute the government's or Parliament's wisdom in proceeding with the program in this fashion rather than at a much slower pace.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-NEW PROCEDURES TO EXPEDITE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-NEW PROCEDURES TO EXPEDITE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 13 of this year I had occasion to question the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) concerning a more expeditious way of handling UIC payments. His answer was helpful and encouraging to some extent, but unfortunately it did not go far enough. There is a real problem in this country concerning the situation with regard to UIC benefits. It is not a subject which should be made a matter of political partisanship. It concerns all members and all parties. This evening I should like to put forward a few suggestions which I hope the minister or his representatives may look at in good faith.
In my constituency of Central Nova we have what I consider to be a unique problem. It is similar in many respects to that in the city of Sydney, Nova Scotia, where the department has taken a second look at the problem which exists in this particular area of the province and, as I understand it, has kept the Sydney office open, or at least it is largely undisturbed. I strongly urge the minister
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
to take a second look at the Pictou County area of my constituency where we have heavy industry, a lot of labour unions and a lot of people adversely affected by the government's policy on this matter.
I do not like to take my allotted time reading things into the record, Mr. Speaker, but I do wish to quote from a letter sent by one of our municipal clerks which sums up the situation admirably. In her letter she states:
I have taken the matter up with our welfare officer and she informs me that under the present system at least four weeks elapse before the cheques are received. This period has, at times, been extended to nine weeks.
A great deal of the money expended for welfare in this county is spent on families who are waiting for their unemployment insurance cheque. In this day and age practically no families can finance themselves for from four to nine weeks.
Our welfare costs this year have greatly exceeded the costs of previous years and also greatly exceeded our estimates.
If anything can be done to shorten the waiting period, it certainly would be of great assistance in lessening the tremendous welfare costs which we are now up against.
The letter is from Helen Carson, municipal clerk of the municipality of Pictou County. The minister has received numerous representations from labour groups in my constituency. He has received telegrams and messages dating back to last spring when he was warned of the chaos that would result from closing the regional office in New Glasgow, or at least from making drastic changes in it.
Having said that, I would like to make a few suggestions. First of all, Mr. Speaker, it seems rather incongruous to me that with regard to the Income Tax Act a citizen of this country is in effect put on the honour system. When he applies for a driver's licence he is put on the honour system. As far as the UIC system itself is concerned, his interim statement or bi-weekly statement of his eligibility is taken, and yet as far as his original acceptability is concerned it appears that the administrative and investigative waiting period is largely the reason why there is so much unacceptable delay.
I would like to suggest that this waiting period, if it is attributable to the necessity to investigate people, be eliminated and that a person be permitted to sign an affidavit so that his benefits can start as soon as the necessary deemed period, whatever it may be in the government's opinion, has passed. If the applicability or suitability for the recipient's benefit is to be examined, let it be examined on the government's time instead of the time of the working man who is waiting for those benefits which he feels are due to him.
Another thing that concerns me is what I consider the perversion that is being used in regard to vacation with pay acts across this country. If a person has benefits accruing to him, it often means that his UIC benefits do not start until the waiting period occasioned by vacation pay lapses. The minister had something to say about that in the House today. The incongruity is that if a person receives the benefits some time before a lay-off occurs, then no waiting period is imposed in respect of funds made available to him when laid off.
I suppose that in future, labour organizers and union negotiators will make sure that the vacation with pay is made available on an accrual basis so that it is not includ-

December 20, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
ed in the waiting period for the UIC benefits. It seems strange that a person could have $5,000 in the bank and receive UIC benefits or receive vacation pay moneys before he is laid off without undue interruption, but if $400 or $500 is due when his employment ceases he must wait until it is used up before the UIC benefit starts. If this is not bad enough, he must also wait four or five weeks after the benefits he has been allocated through vacation pay expire, once it is used up.
Surely there is no reason why, while he is receiving the moneys from his employer which represent his vacation pay and waiting for UIC, the administrative investigation could not be done then so that as soon as the vacation pay is used up he could begin receiving the UIC benefits. I think this is inexcusable. It seems to me analogous to what happened at DEVCO where the UIC Act was used to supplement DEVCO legislation. Here we have vacation pay used in effect to at least supplement if not modify provisions of the UIC regulations.
In this day and age, Mr. Speaker, I see no reason why a person who is going to receive unemployment insurance benefits should not receive them immediately. I do not see why a person's simple affidavit or declaration would not be sufficient to determine his eligibility. If people are dishonest, then they can be caught while benefits are being paid to them and can be prosecuted in the same way as under the Income Tax Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-NEW PROCEDURES TO EXPEDITE PAYMENT OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the minister stated that shortly he hoped to be in a position to describe in more detail procedures designed to speed unemployment insurance benefit payments. However, the Unemployment Insurance Act (1971), section 48(2) provides for assignment of benefits to provincial government or municipal authorities. I can tell the House, Mr. Speaker, that officials of the Unemployment Insurance Commission have completed detailed discussions with all provincial governments in this regard and agreement has been reached on the administrative procedures that will be followed.
Briefly, the procedure will be that when an individual presents himself at a welfare agency with a request for financial assistance because his unemployment insurance claim has been delayed, the welfare officer will establish contact with the Unemployment Insurance Commission district office involved. If it is determined that a claim has been or will be delayed beyond four weeks through no fault of the claimant, the welfare officer can suggest to the claimant that he assign his entitlement to benefit to the agency for the week or weeks concerned. Each month the Unemployment Insurance Commission will send a list to the province showing details of the assignments that have been honoured, together with a cheque to cover the total amount. The details on the list will permit distribution to the local agencies concerned.
It is noteworthy that this procedure does not provide for assignment at the discretion of the welfare officer, but I am sure hon. members would agree that it does permit control over the possibility of duplication of payments.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT TO ENSURE STRICTER CONTROL OVER GUNS IN LIGHT OF MURDER INCREASE
CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT TO ENSURE STRICTER CONTROL OVER GUNS IN LIGHT OF MURDER INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) if he was considering amendments to the Criminal Code to restrict the availability of firearms and other dangerous weapons. The minister replied that the government and Parliament has taken serious action on this matter in 1968 and 1969 when we passed the Criminal Code omnibus bill. It is true that we took action on this matter in 1969 and that we passed amendments at that time which went in the right direction. However, I do not think they went far enough. I said so at the time and I repeat this tonight.
Last Thursday, a 35-year old Montreal policeman, Constable Jean-Guy Sabourin, was shot by a bandit with a machine-gun. This tragic incident took place when three bandits had just finished robbing Simpsons' department store in downtown Montreal. One might ask where these bandits got a machine-gun. Would the police constable have died if the machine-gun had not been available? Would the bandits have attempted the robbery if such weapons were not available?
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the easy availability of dangerous weapons in this country is a scandal. There is no reason for it. It is a strange society where there is more control over the licensing of cars and car drivers than over weapons and there is more control over the sale of liquor than there is over the sale of guns and ammunition. Just down the street, here in Ottawa, a store has set out guns in its window as possible Christmas gifts.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT TO ENSURE STRICTER CONTROL OVER GUNS IN LIGHT OF MURDER INCREASE
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT TO ENSURE STRICTER CONTROL OVER GUNS IN LIGHT OF MURDER INCREASE
speechtext:
Earlier this fall I presented a motion in the House of Commons to have the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs conduct an investigation into the nature and causes of violent crimes in Canada and to report proposals to the House of Commons for correcting this situation. One of the matters that I would expect such an investigation to deal with is the availability and control of weapons. There are also many other matters it could deal with. I still urge the government to initiate such an investigation. In the meantime, however, I strongly urge the government to tighten up the control of dangerous weapons.
In particular, I should like to make the following suggestions. First, all firearms should be sold by retail only through government stores run under a gun control agency. Perhaps this agency could be under the authority of the RCMP or the Attorneys General of the provinces. Second, they should only be sold on application and there should be a delay of perhaps one or two weeks between the receipt of the application and the sale of the gun. There should be a separate application for each weapon, and there should not be a general permit to carry weapons for all purposes. Third, all such applications should be distributed to the police authorities and they should be given public notice. Citizens and public authorities should be allowed to file objections to any such sale or permit. Fourth, applications for sale should only be granted after the applicant has passed a test indicating that (a) he
December 20, 1971

knows how to handle the weapon properly and safely; (b) that he knows the different laws and regulations relating to firearms, and (c) that he has assured the authorities that he needs the weapon for the defined legal purposes set out in the law.
Fifth, the application should only be granted where the applicant needs the weapon as a peace officer, where he needs it to hunt for his food and clothing, when he wishes to hunt for sporting purposes under controlled conditions or where he needs it to protect his life and property, in certain cases. Sixth, the holder of a permit for a firearm should file a report with the gun control agency each year indicating the use and present condition of the weapon. Seventh, no holder of any firearm should be allowed to sell, trade or give away a weapon. Once a weapon is no longer required, it should be turned back to the government-run gun control agency.
Eighth, under no circumstances should a person other than a peace officer be allowed to own, possess or use a handweapon, shortened rifle or shotgun or rapid-fire gun such as a machine-gun. These weapons are presently described as restricted weapons. I feel they should be described as prohibited weapons except for peace officers. Ninth, no one should be allowed to manufacture or import firearms unless they have the strict authorization of the government gun control agency.
Many people will state that these rules are not necessary, that they go too far and nothing is wrong with having a gun if it is used properly. It is probably true that most people who have guns are no threat to society, but on the other hand we have to measure the balance of benefits to society in permitting or restricting the availability of weapons. Despite the fact most people use weapons properly, we are still faced with the situation that they are too available for those who wish to use them for criminal purposes, such as happened last week.
Consequently, I suggest there is greater benefit to be gained by society in a stricter control of these weapons than the benefit now enjoyed by those who use guns under the present law. If such a law saved only one life per year, such as that of Constable Sabourin, it would be
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
well worth it and would compensate for the inconvenience of those who do not have the full availability of guns.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Bechard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT TO ENSURE STRICTER CONTROL OVER GUNS IN LIGHT OF MURDER INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I think, first of all, my two colleagues from Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) and Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) who constitute a most inspiring audience.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) brought up a matter from which stems the terrible tragedy which occurred last week in Montreal when police agent Jean-Guy Sabourin, in the course of his duties as agent of the peace, was savagely slain by a gangster armed with a submachine gun.
On behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and on my own behalf, I wish to offer Mrs. Sabourin and her three young children, as well as the other members of the family, our heartfelt and most sincere condolences.
The minister and the government are genuinely concerned with savage acts perpetrated against those who are invested with the duty of protecting society, people and goods.
The hon. member does know that in 1969, thanks to the present government and to the Minister of Justice in particular, substantial amendments were made to the Criminal Code in connection with firearms and particularly those with restricted uses like machine guns.
In this regard I shall refer the hon. member to section 83 of the Criminal Code and the following sections with which he is well acquainted and which appear in the 1970 edition.
When these amendments were being prepared, the idea of general registration of all firearms was examined from every angle and the RCMP was consulted in this respect. However, the conclusion arrived at was that such a procedure would be difficult if not impossible to enforce.
We appreciate the difficulty of producing faultless legislation whether in the field of criminal law or in any other. There will inevitably be imperfections.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would assure the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that I shall consider it a duty to pass on his suggestions to the Minister of Justice.
